Title: Pidato Deputi Gubernur, Muliaman D. Hadad Pada Peresmian BMSI Sebagai Bank Penerima Setoran Biaya Penyelenggaraan Ibadah Haji dan Launching Produk Tabungan Haji iB
text: Deputy Governor's Welcome Pointers At the Inauguration of BMSI as a Bank receiving deposit fees for organizing hajj (BPIH) and launching of Hajj Savings Products iB Jakarta, July 24, 2009 Which we respect, - Minister of Religious Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia, Mr. Muh. Maftuh Basyuni - Senior Advisor PT. Bank Syariah Mega Indonesia, Mr. Chairul Tanjung - Managing Director of PT. BSMI, Mr. Beny Witjaksono, - Attendees invited Assalamu'alaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh Introduction : Expression of gratitude and congratulations to BSMI 1. Thank God , let us always pray for the presence of Allah SWT because tonight we can all stay in touch and witness the inauguration of PT. Mega Syariah Indonesia (BMSI) as the bank receiving the deposit of hajj implementation fees (BPIH) and at the same time launching the iB BSMI Hajj savings product. 2. I would like to congratulate Bank Mega Syariah on the appointment as the recipient bank for hajj deposits (BPIH) and also on the launch of the IB Hajj savings product from Bank Mega Syariah. 3. Future expectations: - Maintaining and increasing the trust given by the Government to BMSI as the bank receiving the BPIH deposit -, among others, by improving service quality, service counters, IT, and professional human resources. - Increased innovation in features and product variety as well as convenience for customers on iB Hajj savings products - followed by promotions and adequate product knowledge - In the future, with the resources, capability and accumulated business experience owned by BMSI - it is hoped that BMSI can continue to increase its role and contribution in the development of the Islamic economy in the country once upon a time in the economy. Current Challenges of the Islamic Bank Industry: Macro and Micro 4. We are grateful because in the midst of the environment after the global financial crisis, the national economy is still stable and growing positively. On the other hand, shariah finance in the country (has been present since 1992) continues to show progress even though it needs to be accelerated again: - The expansion of the industry continues to take place the Islamic industry is still 'attractive' the number of 'players' is increasing and the average growth of the number of Islamic banking offices during the The last 4 years reach up to 24%. In the future , there will be more BUS and UUS. - Encouraging financial performance indicators of growth in assets, deposits, and financing/financing which on average/year reached above 30% (Note, Assets: 36%, Deposits: 32% and financing: 37%). Similarly, the fund disbursement ratio (FDR) reached 104%, while roe reached 62% per year. 5. Some issues/challenges at the macro level : - The issue of financial stability and the role of sharia finance issues after the global financial crisis: building confidence, financing/credit flow lines opened, financial market efficiency, real value of assets, risk management, and innovation product advantages of shari'a finance: non-speculative. based on underlying assets, a clear link with assets. - The share of Islamic financial assets is still relatively small at 2.2% requiring concerted efforts from the government, regulators, and industry players as well as supporting s takeholders - Competition in the Islamic banking industry is increasing in the national financial industry and regional and global Islamic industries. 6. Some issues/challenges at the micro industry level: - Competition among Islamic banks is increasing "players" in BUS/UUS in industries that are still in the stage of developing/expanding the competition-cooperative /aliances paradigm. - Product and service innovations mostly in skim murabahah (buying and selling) need speed to respond to customer needs and create benefits and value for customers BI provisions that provide more flexibility in the issuance of products - The HR aspect is good in terms of quantity and quality. Directions of market and product development strategies 7. As a new form of banking services, national Islamic banking needs to be "creatively" to continue to develop marketing strategies that can encourage sustainable growth and increase the participation of Islamic banking to support the national economy. 8. In relation to the development of the Islamic banking market, Bank Indonesia together with Islamic banking industry players have formulated a strategy to realize a new image of Islamic banking, namely "Sharia Bank - More than Just a Bank" (or beyond banking), which is described as a bank whose services cross various diversity, with a wealth of types of products and services, as well as various variations of financing schemes. 9. Related to that, development efforts are one of the important priorities that need to be carried out by national Islamic banks. The product development program, in addition to being an effort to meet the various demands of business needs and the use of banking services in general, is also a way to support the uniqueness of Islamic banking that has a diversity of products with varied schemes. 10. The development of Islamic banking products needs to consider various business aspects such as: - features that attract and benefit customers, - flexible and in accordance with the needs of the business world and service users in general, - the level of risk that can be calculated and managed properly, - comply with basic norms and sharia principles. In essence, Islamic banking products need to reflect the positioning of Islamic banking that is mutually beneficial to both parties. 11. In relation to product development strategies, a number of recommendations have been submitted by marketing experts, including: - Efforts to introduce syraiah banking products should use branding or certainty that is easy for the average public to understand. - In addition to an effective communication approach, Islamic banks need to continue to innovate and take new steps for product channeling in order to commercialize their products and services. The concept of 'office channeling' is a breakthrough for efficient product channeling. - In addition, investment in the provision of information technology-based banking services such as ATMs, mobile banking, internet banking, e-money and others is a necessity in today's banking market competition. Hajj: Opportunities and Roles of Islamic Banking 12. Opportunities and role of Islamic banking in Hajj services - Hajj is a pillar of Islam that is rich in meaning both in terms of flosophical and sharia. There is a 'wisdom' implied by some islamic teachings for the ummah, especially the Hajj: (a) the paradigm of going global muslims must be mobile through the transfer of resources (intangible and tangible), outward looking, part of the community dunia. (b) Islamic ummah must be empowered / master resources and competencies in order to facilitate their worship - e.g. : hajj requires transportation (airlines, modes of transportation, buses), communication (cellphone communication tools etc.), accommodation (hotels, catering, etc.), teknologi (computer, IT, etc.) - the fact: hajj is a worship that belongs to Muslims, but the supplier of facilities and who obtains benefits mostly non-islamic (planes, hotels, communication channels, etc.) - There are great opportunities in niche markets related to worship such as Hajj, zakat, and waqf 13. Regarding the appointment as the bank receiving the deposit of the hajj -, BI hopes that BSMI can carry out the mandate and provide the best service for the cal on allah guests. In this regard, conceptually there has been a thought that Islamic banks should take the largest role in the receipt and management of Hajj funds. It seems commonplace that financial management for activities related to worship activities such as the implementation of haji financial management is fully carried out by Islamic banks. 14. From the perspective of islamic banking development, this should be a "challenge and encouragement" to be able to improve operational efficiency, service quality, the sophistication of information technology applications and network expansion in order to meet the demands of the government as the organizer of the hajj implementation. So that from one time the role of syraiah banks as recipients and managers of Hajj funds can continue to increase. Closing Remarks: 15. Pleasehope that Islamic banking industry players, especially Bank Mega Syariah, continue to significantly strengthen their capacity and capabilities in order to respond to the challenges and environment faced current and future. 16. With the various point above, I would like to close my remarks and once again congratulate BMSI as the bank receiving BPIH deposits and also the launching of the Hajj Savings product. May Allah Almighty always be pleased to give His mercy and blessings to all of us. That's it and thank you Billahittaufiq wal hidayah Wassalamu'alaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh Jakarta, 24th July 2009 Muliaman D. Hadad Deputy Governor
text_original: Pointers Sambutan Deputi Gubernur Pada Peresmian BMSI Sebagai Bank Penerima Setoran Biaya Penyelenggaraan Ibadah Haji (BPIH) dan Launching Produk Tabungan Haji iB Jakarta, 24 Juli 2009 Yang kami hormati, - Menteri Agama RI, Bapak Muh. Maftuh Basyuni - Senior Advisor PT. Bank Syariah Mega Indonesia, Bapak Chairul Tanjung - Dirut PT. BSMI, Pak Beny Witjaksono, - Para undangan hadirin hadirat Assalamu'alaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh Pendahuluan : Ungkapan syukur dan selamat kepada BSMI 1. Syukur alhamdulillah mari kita senantiasa panjatkan kehadirat Allah SWT karena pada malam ini kita semua dapat bersilaturahmi dan menyaksikan peresmian PT. Mega Syariah Indonesia (BMSI) sebagai bank penerima setoran biaya penyelenggaraan ibadah haji (BPIH) dan sekaligus launching produk tabungan haji iB BSMI. 2. Saya ingin menyampaikan selamat atas penunjukkan Bank Mega Syariah sebagai bank penerima setoran ibadah haji (BPIH) dan juga atas peluncuran produk tabungan haji IB dari Bank Mega Syariah. 3. Harapan kedepan: - Menjaga dan meningkatkan kepercayaan yang diberikan Pemerintah kepada BMSI sebagai bank penerima setoran BPIH tersebut -> antara lain dengan peningkatan service quality, counter pelayanan, IT, dan SDM yang profesional. - Peningkatan inovasi pada feature dan ragam produk serta kemudahan bagi nasabah pada produk tabungan iB haji -> diikuti dengan promosi dan produk knowledge yang memadai - Ke depan, dengan resources, capability dan akumulasi pengalaman bisnis yang dimiliki BMSI -> diharapkan BMSI dapat terus meningkatkan role dan kontribusi dalam pengembangan ekonomi syariah di tanah air sekalius pada perekonomian. Tantangan Industri Bank Syariah Saat Ini: Makro dan Mikro 4. Kita bersyukur karena di tengah environment pasca krisis finansial global perekonomian nasional masih stabil dan tumbuh positif. Disisi lain, shariah finance di tanah air (sudah hadir sejak tahun 1992) terus memperlihatkan kemajuan meski butuh diakselerasi lagi: - Ekspansi industri terus berlangsung industri syariah masih 'atraktif' jumlah 'pemain' bertambah dan pertumbuhan rata-rata jumlah kantor perbankan syariah selama 4 tahun terakhir mencapai hingga 24%. Ke depan akan bertambah BUS dan UUS nya. - Indikator kinerja keuangan yang menggembirakan growth aset, DPK, dan pembiayaan/financing yang rata-rata/tahun mencapai di atas 30% (Catatan, Aset: 36%, DPK : 32% dan pembiayaan : 37%). Demikian pula dengan rasio penyaluran dana (FDR) mencapai 104%, sedangkan ROE mencapai 62% per tahun. 5. Beberapa isu/tantangan di level makro : - Isu financial stability dan peran syariah finance isu pasca krisis finansial global : membangun confidence, line arus pembiayaan/kredit dibuka, efisiensi financial market, real value dari aset, risk management, serta inovasi product keunggulan syarih finance : non-speculative. berbasisi underlying asset, link yang jelas dengan aset. - Share aset keuangan syariah masih relatif kecil 2,2% butuh concerted effort dari pemerintah, regulator, dan pelaku industri serta stakeholder pendukung - Kompetisi industri perbankan syariah meningkat terhadap industri keuangan nasional dan industri syariah regional dan global. 6. Beberapa isu/tantangan di level mikro industri : - Persaingan diantara bank syariah bertambah "pemain" di BUS/UUS dalam industri yang masih dalam stage pengembangan/ekspansi paradigma kompetisi-kooperasi /aliances. - Inovasi produk dan layanan sebagian besar dalam skim murabahah (jual beli) butuh kecepatan untuk merespon need nasabah dan menciptakan benefit dan value bagi nasabah ketentuan BI yang lebih memberikan keleluasaan dalam penerbitan priduk - Aspek SDM baik dari sisi kuantitas dan kualitas. Arah strategi pengembangan pasar dan produk 7. Sebagai suatu bentuk layanan jasa perbankan yang baru perbankan syariah nasional perlu "secara kreatif" untuk terus mengembangkan strategi marketing yang dapat mendorong pertumbuhan yang berkesinambungan dan peningkatan peran serta perbankan syariah mendukung perekonomian nasional. 8. Terkait dengan pengembangan pasar perbankan syariah ini Bank Indonesia bersama dengan pelaku industry perbankan syariah telah merumuskan suatu strategi untuk mewujudkan citra baru perbankan syariah yaitu "Bank Syariah - Lebih dari Sekedar Bank" (atau beyond banking), yang dideskripsikan sebagai bank yang jasa pelayanannya melintasi berbagai keragaman, dengan kekayaan jenis produk dan jasa, serta berbagai variasi skema pembiayaan. 9. Terkait dengan itu maka upaya-upaya pengembangan menjadi salah satu prioritas penting yang perlu dilakukan perbankan syariah nasional. Program pengembangan produk selain merupakan upaya untuk memenuhi berbagai tuntutan kebutuhan bisnis dan penguna jasa perbankan secara umum juga merupakan suatu jalan untuk menkongkretkan keunikan perbankan syariah yang memiliki keragaman produk dengan skema variatif. 10. Pengembangan produk perbankan syariah perlu mempertimbangkan berbagai aspek bisnis seperti : - features yang menarik dan menguntungkan nasabah, - fleksibel dan sesuai dengan kebutuhan dunia usaha dan pengguna jasa secara umum, - tingkat risiko yang dapat dikalkulasi dan dikelola secara baik, - comply dengan norma dasar dan prinsip syariah. Pada intinya produk-produk perbankan syariah perlu merefleksikan positioning perbankan syariah yang saling menguntungkan kedua belah pihak. 11. Dalam kaitan strategi pengembangan produk sejumlah rekomendasi telah disampaikan oleh ahli pemasaran antara lain : - Upaya pengenalan produk perbankan syraiah sebaiknya menggunakan branding atau persitilahan yang mudah difahami masyarakat kebanyakan. - Selain pendekatan komunikasi yang efektif, bank-bank syariah perlu terus melakukan inovasi dan langkah baru untuk product channeling dalam rangka komersialisasi produk dan layanan jasanya. Konsep 'office channeling' merupakan suatu terobosan untuk channeling produk dengan efisien. - Selain itu investasi untuk penyediaan layanan perbankan berbasis teknologi informasi seperti ATM, mobile banking, internet banking, e-money dan lain-lain merupakan sebuah keniscayaan dalam persaingan pasar perbankan dewasa ini. Haji: Peluang dan Peran Perbankan Syariah 12. Peluang dan peran perbankan syariah dalam layanan haji - Haji merupakan rukun islam yang kaya makna baik dari sisi flosofis maupun syariahnya. Terdapat 'hikmah' yang tersirat dari beberapa ajaran islam bagi ummat, khususnya haji : (a) paradigma go global umat islam harus mobile melalui transfer resources (intangible maupun tangible), berpikiran outward looking, bagian dari komunitas dunia. (b) ummat islam harus berdaya/menguasai resources dan competencies agar dapat menfasilitasi ibadahnya -> mis : haji membutuhkan transportasi (airlines, moda transportasi, bus), komunikasi (alat komunikasi hp dll), akomodasi (hotel, catering, dll), teknologi (komputer, IT, dll) -> faktanya : haji adalah ibadah milik umat islam, tapi penyuplai sarana dan yang memperoleh benefit sebagian besar non islam (pesawat, hotel, saluran komunikasi, dll) - Terdapat peluang yang besar dalam niche market yang terkait ibadah seperti haji, zakat, dan wakaf 13. Terkait dengan penunjukan sebagai bank penerima setoran biaya penyelenggaraan haji -> , BI berharap BSMI dapat menjalankan amanah dan memberikan layanan jasa terbaik bagi para cal on tamu Allah. Dalam kaitan ini, secara konsepsional selama ini ada pemikiran agar bank-bank syariah mengambil peran terbesar dalam penerimaan dan pengelolaan dana haji. Agaknya lumrah bahwa pengelolaan keuangan untuk kegiatan yang terkait dengan aktivitas ibadah seperti pelaksanaan haji pengelolaan keuangannya sepenuhnya dilaksanakan oleh bank-bank syariah. 14. Dari perspektif pengembangan perbankan syariah ini seharusnya menjadi "tantangan dan pemacu semangat" untuk dapat meningkatkan efisiensi operasi, kualitas layanan, kecanggihan aplikasi teknologi informasi dan perluasan jaringan agar dapat memenuhi tuntutan pemerintah selaku penyelenggara pelaksanaan haji. Sehingga dari watu kewaktu peran perbankan syraiah sebagai penerima dan pengelola dana haji dapat terus meningkat. Penutup: 15. Harapan agar pelaku industri perbankan syariah, khususnya Bank Mega Syariah, terus melanjutkan langkah penguatan capacity dan capabilities nya secara signifikan agar dapat merespon tantangan dan environment yang dihadapi saat ini dan ke depan. 16. Dengan berbagai point di atas, saya ingin menutup sambutan saya ini dan sekali lagi menyampaikan selamat atas penunjukan BMSI sebagai bank penerima setoran BPIH dan juga launching produk Tabungan Haji. Semoga Allah SWT senantiasa berkenan memberikan rahmat dan ridha-Nya kepada kita sekalian. Sekian dan terima kasih Billahittaufiq wal hidayah Wassalamu'alaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh Jakarta, 24 Juli 2009 Muliaman D. Hadad Deputi Gubernur

Title: Keynote Speech SEACEN Payment System Directors' Meeting - Yogyakarta, November 29, 2007 (S. Budi Rochadi - Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia)
text: Keynote Speech SEACEN PAYMENT SYSTEM DIRECTORS MEETING Yogyakarta, November 29, 2007 S. BUDI ROCHADI DEPUTY GOVERNOR, BANK INDONESIA Distinguished Mrs. Lim Lai Hong, the Director of Training and Administrator, SEACEN Centre Distinguished Payment System Directors from all SEACEN and observing countries, Distinguished Speakers, Ladies and Gentlemen, Good afternoon, Assalamualaikum wr.wb, may the blessing of the Almighty be bestowed upon all of us. Welcome to Yogyakarta! Almost a year ago, I was appointed as Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor. With the appointment the payment system has become part of my responsibilities, besides the currency circulation and two other sectors namely rural bank supervision and credit. The payment system and currency circulation are two different areas involving different methods of payments and different payment instruments, each with its own challenges which are quite different from one another. Our Payment System Department has brought to me many plans for the future. One of the plans is building the second generation of Bank Indonesia RTGS System. When we look around the region, we can see that some of our colleagues, like the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Bank of Thailand, and the Reserve Bank of Australia, have finished bringing their 2nd generation RTGS to live. At the present, Bank Indonesia is on the way to do the same. This development, we believe, is not triggered merely by system obsolescence but more than that, the new system is aimed to provide the whole banking industry and the economy with a much more efficient system. A new system which allows more liquidity savings, lower costs of access for small banks, lower investment outlay and more robust back up facilities. Hopefully, overall it will be less costly to the economy. This of course directly supports one of Bank 1 Indonesias mandates that is ensuring the smooth functioning of payment systems, which is of utmost importance to support the financial system and monetary stability. Therefore the first theme of this meeting, which emphasizes on the evolution of large-value payment systems, will be highly beneficial for us. Moreover it will also benefit those who are planning to revamp their current RTGS setups, and even to those who just start the first generations. Ladies and Gentlemen, The second theme, which is on retail payment landscape, is also a great policy subject. Within Bank Indonesia we have been discussing many policy issues including that of regulating the issuance of e-money, both issued by banks and by non-bank non-financial institutions. The introduction of e-money is a logical consequence of the advancement of technology, which is supposed to make our lives easier. However, to regulators like us new technology such as emoney besides being a blessing, it could also impose new challenges. Some of the challenges would arise when the time comes when people start using e-money for economic transactions across the borders of countries. Although it might be too early to predict, I have a feeling that there would be some aspect of e-money that may require cross-border collaboration amongst payment system regulators and overseers. Hence, directors meeting such as this one that is organized by SEACEN Centre can become an ideal forum for such collaboration. Ladies and Gentlemen, Another policy issue in retail payments that has been brought forth within Bank Indonesia this year is How to bring the industry to become more collaborative instead of merely competitive, and how to make the industry to start regulating themselves, or in other words, to become selfregulatory. Examples from various parts of the world have shown that the private sector can and will self regulate if they are given the opportunity and enough push and nudging, and also ample support by the regulators. Of course, last but not least, the self-regulatory industry shall be subjected to strong oversight by the regulators, or otherwise they may abuse their newfound power. Self-regulations by the industry shall even include the industrys collaboration to ensure customer education and protection from getting abused by the industry itself. I understand that it 2 may sound like a tall order, because it may not be so easy for the industry to put fines and charges on its own members for not protecting their own customers. This is of course very different from the relationship between regulators and industry which is under the coverage of public law. Nevertheless if we are to grow an industry that is healthy and responsible, it may worth trying new formula. We have to keep in mind though that the regulators still need to have very strong hold on the industry, and not loosening up unless the industry has proven itself. Again I am very sure that SEACEN Payment System Directors Meeting is an excellent forum within which we can sit together and discuss many policy issues. It is a forum where advises from colleagues can be sought after, and perhaps one day it may evolve to become a forum to resolve policy issues of common interests to all participating central banks. So Ladies and Gentlemen, As I am nearing to the end of my speech this afternoon, I would like to again welcome you all to this historical city of Yogyakarta. I hope you are all well taken care of, and have the chance to see the beauty of the city and its ancient monuments and also to get good bargains on local arts and crafts. Please do not hesitate to contact any of our staff on the ground for any assistance that you may need. I wish you all a fruitful and productive meeting. Good Afternoon Wassalamualaikum wr.wb 3

Title: Keynote Speech by Acting Governor of Bank Indonesia, Miranda S. Goeltom at the 7th Bank Indonesia Annual International Seminar "Global Financial Tsunami: What Can We Do?"
text: DEALING WITH GLOBAL FINANCIAL CRISES Welcome Remarks by Miranda S. Goeltom, Acting Governor, the Central Bank of Indonesia, delivered at the 7th Bank Indonesia Annual International Seminar Global Financial Tsunami: What Can We Do? Nusa Dua, Bali, June 13-14, 2009 Honorable Minister Indrawati, Gov. Atiur Rachman, and Jacob Frenkel, Distinguished Speakers, Guests and Participants, Ladies and Gentlemen, Good afternoon and greeting to you all, It is indeed an honor and a great pleasure for me to welcome all of you to this the 7th Bank Indonesia Annual International Seminar, entitled Global Financial Tsunami: What Can We Do?. Let me also welcome our distinguished guests and participants from abroad to our country and especially to Bali. I hope that you will have the time to experience this beautiful island while you are here. I also extend sincere gratitude and thanks to all speakers who will share their valuable time and insights over the next two days. Ladies and Gentlemen, Global Financial Crisis We are meeting today in challenging times. The global economy is being drawn deeper into the most serious crisis in our life time. So devastating has the global financial crisis been it was billed as the most dramatic since the Great Depression of the 1930s. The most commonly used objective to describe the current financial crisis is unprecedented. It is unprecedented in terms of speed at which events unfolded and triggered a series of domino effects, the scale of the impact 1 which has become global, and the range of unconventional measures taken by authorities around the world. This has been demonstrated in the policy responses taken to overcome the crisis, which is incredibly complex and certainly costly. IMF projected global economic growth to plummet from 3.2% in 2008 to -1.3% in 2009, whereas economic growth in developed countries is estimated to be even worse, contracting to -3.8%. IMF also predicted that total losses stemming from the current global financial crisis will reach US4 trillion, two-thirds of which is from the banking sector. In such a deep global crisis, we must seek ways to survive and, subsequently, return to our previously hard won growth and stability. This is exactly the time when collective action is needed most, so that we can survive this global financial tsunami, and emerge stronger. Given the depth and systemic nature of the crisis, a wait-and-see approach or simply hoping that recovery will take place on its own is utterly unacceptable. Ladies and Gentlemen, Common Historical Perspective of the Crisis In the past, when the world caught a cold, Indonesia and countries in the region got pneumonia; today it is the other way around, our countries got a cold while the developed world is suffering from bird-flu. While Indonesia and countries in the region have withstood the effect of an international crisis like never before, that is no reason for complacency. History teaches us that various crises have occurred repeatedly in line with the natural business cycle. We recognize several types of financial crisis, such as a currency crisis, debt crisis or banking crisis. Examples of a currency crisis include the ones that plagued countries under the European Monetary System (EMS) in 1992-93 and Mexico in 1994-95; debt crises ravaged Mexico in 1973-82 and Argentina in 2 1978-81 and 2001-02, as well as Russia and Brazil in 1998-99; and banking crises beset countries across Europe and the US in the 19th century and early 20th century. On several occasions, banking crises were also accompanied by a currency crisis, such as that which struck East Asian countries: Thailand, Korea, Malaysia and Indonesia in 1997-98. This phenomenon of a currency crisis and concomitant banking crisis became known as a twin-crisis. Globally, with increasing synergy between macroeconomic variables, crises have become multidimensional, which is true for the ongoing global financial crisis. Meanwhile, the length of the cycle and duration of its effects are basically identifiable. From a number of empirical facts it can be concluded that although crises are occurring repeatedly, there is no indication that they will transpire periodically, as a characteristic of the actual business cycle itself. However, empirical observations of Western European history over the last 400 years show that financial crises occur, on average, at approximately 10-year intervals. Meanwhile, regarding the economic recovery process out of a financial crisis, a recent study demonstrates that a deep and protracted financial crisis affects the price of assets, output growth and level of unemployment. In this case, the affect of a financial crisis on a decline in employment and house prices lasts an average of 5 to 6 years, whereas the affect on output is shorter at an average of 2 years. The current global financial crisis is a stark warning to us concerning how the dynamics of the global economy and its risks are highly interconnected. In this case, contagion not only spreads through linkages in trade and finance but also through complex interaction among various risks, as depicted in the near-perfect correlation of market and asset classes that was uncorrelated when conditions were benign, and eventually amplified uncertainty and lead to a more difficult decision-making process. While there are numerous cases that can explain why and how financial crises transpire, there are many fundamental issues that we are yet to understand. To this end, a number of arduous challenges have emerged from the ongoing global financial 3 crisis that force public authorities to institute not only short-term but also long-term policy responses. Ladies and Gentlemen, Policy Responses We are all in the agreement that the global crisis requires a global solution. Global concerted action is thus needed to offset a further worldwide recession by organizing collaborative fiscal stimuli to boost public and private demand. Global cooperation should also be expanded from the financial sector to the real sector in order to provide more comprehensive measures for the recovery of global economic growth. Efforts should be made to enhance cooperation in trade financing, and step up cooperation at the regional and international level. For policymakers, the unprecedented challenge is to avert a deeper recession. What has deeply concerned us, every policymaker worldwide, and is to be avoided at almost any cost, is the vicious downward spiral between the financial sector and real sector. Amidst such ramifications and negative feedback, we need to anticipate that this unfolding crisis will take considerably longer than previously envisaged. In my opinion, it is of utmost importance to seek deeper understanding of at least three interrelated issues: (1) the underlying structural weaknesses, (2) the merit of policy response; and (3) the underdeveloped institutional structure and system. Those three issues, I believe, are inherent in this ongoing crisis. Much has been accomplished. Wide-ranging and often unconventional policy responses have been taken to contain the downturn in output. In the near term, we are already doing much involving the provision of fiscal stimuli and liquidity to contain the financial crisis. While underlining the importance of fiscal stimuli, we also need to ensure long-term fiscal sustainability. Along with this, measures to repair and reinforce the financial sector must be taken. This medium-term measure is vital in order to prevent a similar situation in the future and to provide sustainable economic 4 growth. We must remember that the economy will only recover if supported by a functioning financial sector. Despite the inevitable current preoccupation with the near-term, we also need to remain focused on the structural reforms required to achieve higher sustainable output growth and to strengthen the long-term capacity. With greater potential for unexpected short-term economic risks, policy focus must be anchored towards longterm economic interests. The implementation of such policy signals is our commitment to stay focused on the long-term and press ahead with the structural reform agenda. But, will appropriate macroeconomic policies and a strengthened regulatory and supervisory framework be able to prevent future financial crises? I personally think that we should not simplify the issues and presume that better regulations, more effective supervision and longer-term stability-oriented macroeconomic policy would suffice to eliminate the cyclical features of the financial system and the build-up of financial imbalances in the future. I strongly believe that market participants have an equally important role to play  and self-interest  in addressing some of the emerging weaknesses in the financial system and in strengthening market discipline. In this regard, better flow of information in the market would enable authorities to safeguard financial stability and other prudential aspects, as well as reduce the procyclicality impacts of financial sector behaviour. Therefore, there will be more resilience and we will be better prepared when new shocks hit in the future. Recently, there have been some early signs of success. There is evidence of stability returning to financial markets. It seems that the financial markets are gradually moving back towards conditions that may be able to support the economic recovery when it eventually begins. Global equities climbed to their highest levels of the year, oil rose to around 70 a barrel, the Baltic Dry Index an indicator of shipping activity has risen sixfold from its December nadir and corporate bond spreads narrowed to levels last seen in October 2008, while US-Treasury bond yields 5 touched fresh six-month highs. The latter indicator can be seen as a sign of economic optimism as investors abandon the safety of government bonds for riskier assets. There has been speculation that a trough has possibly been reached in few countries, providing evidence of green shoots. We also witness many signs of a slowing in the pace of contraction and increasing expectations of an economic recovery. These positive financial and economic indicators encouraged hopes that the Great Recession might be coming to an end. Finally, it seems there is a light at the end of the tunnel. Has the crisis reached rock bottom? Have we passed the worst? Is the crisis behind us? And if so, should we now concentrate more on the exit policy and related measures to alleviate the mounting inflationary pressures?? Ladies and Gentlemen, In line with the above empirical and policy perspectives, we are gathering today to confer salient issues that have emerged during the recent financial tsunami. In the first session we will discuss the effects of the global financial crisis on the economy, which differ primarily due to differences in the driving factors behind the crisis. A related issue to be raised here is as follows: are accommodative monetary policy, financial innovation boom and insufficient financial regulation considered as the factors behind the shocks?. Session 2 will discuss further how policymakers can avoid a prolonged slump? Should a new paradigm of monetary and banking system be found to avoid repercusions from the financial crisis? From a market perspective, Session 3 will explore how the development of the financial market has provided a significant contribution to various innovations in advanced financial products, thus triggering moral hazard and escallating asymmetric information in the financial market. As noted, a critical lesson learned from the current crisis is the need for a more rigorous continuity plan in the financial sector. Session 4 will therefore focus on building effective crisis resolution and management covering the wide array of macro and micro-level policy measures. The final session will emphasize key priorities for regaining global financial stability from a country perspective. Several of the 6 presentations will deliver substantial measures for reshaping the future financial system, including the needs to expand the perimeter of financial regulations. Ladies and Gentlemen, Let me conclude my brief remarks by saying that from the point of view of an emerging economy central banker, such as myself, we are indeed living in changing times. Dealing with this global financial crisis is of paramount importance. Many of our working assumptions are constantly being challenged by this new reality. This requires sound policy judgements on our part and, more importantly, courage to implement bold measures which perhaps no one has instituted previously. Therefore, the challenge ahead is to get the action plan implemented expeditiously, decisively and concertedly with equal allertness of the challenges to establish a proper and adequate exit policy. Despite the daunting tasks that we are assuming, I would prefer to remain sanguine. I recognize we need to remain vigilant and stand ready to make changes along the way as we may encounter the unexpected. I sincerely hope that this Seminar will be fruitful in generating valuable insight and new ideas in dealing with global financial crises. Therefore, I guess you will agree with me that it is interesting to listen and learn from the vast experience of a world known economist and former IMF Chief Economist, a noted and well regarded former central bank governor, and Chairman of Group of Thirty, Dr. Jacob Frenkel. Before I close my remarks, let me bring up an interesting note about Bali. The water found here on this paradise island is extremely addictive; once you have tried it once you will succumb to the islands exotic wonders and return time and time again. So, once is never enough. I urge you to make the most of your visit and explore the magnificent sights, tastes and sounds of the island, with the hope that the memories you take away are unforgettable. Thank you, and let me now turn the floor to my dear friend Jacob to deliver his keynote remarks. 7

Title: Building A Better Financial Infrastructure In Asia by Budi Mulya - Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia at SWIFT Business Forum 2010, Jakarta
text: BUILDING A BETTER FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE IN ASIA1 BUDI MULYA Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia Jakarta, 11 May 2010 Distinguished speakers, guest, ladies and gentlemen, Good morning and welcome to this forum. Let us start our discussion today by expressing our gratefulness to God almighty. It is a pleasure to be here and have the opportunity to share with you a topic that is becoming increasingly crucial for the economic development in Asia region. I thank SWIFT for the invitation to join in todays business forum. I would like to focus my remarks in the area with regard to the integration of the economy as well as financial markets in a region, especially in South-East Asia, known as ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) by 2015; and accordingly the importance of harmonization of market infrastructures in ASEAN member countries, to facilitate the more integrated ASEAN market. Let me start with a brief discussion on a rather contradictory view on global financial market integrations. One extreme opinion sustains that integrated financial markets improve the allocation of productive resources, foster entrepreneurship and innovation, enhance market discipline, and help countries to insure against macroeconomic fluctuations. At the other extreme, it is argued that the free flow of capital widens the wealth gap between rich and poor countries and exposes domestic financial markets to the risk of instability, or more vulnerable to external shock. The later, one can observe from the evidence following the most recent global financial market turmoil. In dealing those of the later, relevant policy makers of ASEAN countries obviously must devote great efforts, hand in hand, in making series of key policies aimed at reducing gaps, inequality and income differences across the region, as well as to develop a close coordination measure to mitigate the risk of potential financial market instability. That is about to minimizing the opposing view of financial integrations. 1 Keynotes speech delivered at SWIFT Business Forum 2010, Building a better financial infrastructure in Asia. Jakarta, 11 May 2010. 1 / 4 Ladies and gentlemen, As we notice nowadays, economic and financial globalization has been taking place continuously, mostly in the form of establishment of a regional single market or regional integration of financial markets. All initiatives about a regional integration of countries or financial markets, including the one in South-East Asia called ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) by 2015, are aimed at transforming the regions into regional single markets and production base that are fully integrated and highly competitive into the global community. The economic or market integration in a region includes elimination of tariffs and streamlined customs clearance procedure for facilitating and increasing free flow of goods and services amongst the intra-regional countries, free movement of professionals, as well as freer flow of capital across the region. With regard to ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) by 2015, transforming ASEAN into a region with free movement of goods, services, investment, skilled labor, and freer flow of capital by 2015 means that there will be increasing flow of funds or payments between economic agents located in different countries in ASEAN, and greater intra-ASEAN securities cross border trading. Accordingly, in order to facilitate intra-ASEAN cross-border transactions, complementary policy measures and market infrastructures (for payments and for trading, clearing and settlement of securities), which are harmonized, standardized, thus inter-operable or even inter-linkable across borders, become fundamental requirements. A number of policy researches studying about market infrastructures of regions integrating their intra-regional countries or financial markets, confirm that a single market is correlated with the degree of integration of the related underlying market infrastructures, such as payment systems and securities settlement systems. Moreover, degree of integration of the related payment systems and securities settlement systems of the intra-regional countries depend on, at least, three critical issues namely infrastructure, business process, and legal aspect. They are such that: - whether infrastructures for transfer and settlement of payments and securities in the intra-regional countries are standard (therefore inter-operable or inter-linkable across borders) or not; - whether business practices of operations for transfer and settlement of payments and securities in the intra-regional countries are harmonized or not; and 2 / 4 - whether legal basis of operations for transfer and settlement of payments and securities in the intra-regional countries are harmonized or not. With regard to the use of standard infrastructures for transfer and settlement of payments and securities and according to our data, currently there are 60 real-time gross settlement (RTGS) systems and 95 securities settlement and depository systems in 54 countries. This standard infrastructure includes: a SWIFT message standard for the message formats of the domestic inter-bank high-value payments and securities transfers; and a SWIFT network for highly secure and resilient messaging the domestic inter-bank high-value payments and securities transfers. Since SWIFT is used initially by banks and other financial institutions around the world for messaging transfers of cross-border payments and securities to correspondent abroad, the use of such an open worldwide communication network with (global) standard financial message formats for the domestic inter-bank high-value payments in 60 countries RTGS system, and transfers of securities deposited with securities settlement and depository systems in 54 countries will make participants of those countries involved able to gain the cost efficiency. Those are due to the use of single-window access connection and standard message formats both for messaging transfers of the domestic inter-bank high-value payments and securities; and for messaging transfers of cross-border payments and securities to correspondent banks or financial institutions abroad. Also they gain from efficiency of operation and maintenance of infrastructures at the participants site, including their straight-through processing (STP) infrastructure. Furthermore, the open and common standards relate to the use of International Bank Account Number (IBAN), International Securities Identification Number (ISIN), Bank Identifier Code (BIC), and Universal Financial Industry (UNIFI) Message Scheme. The use of such global standards approved by International Organization for Standardization (ISO) for messaging both domestic and cross-border financial transactions, will lead operations of financial infrastructures in an economy including those at the commercial banks site, efficient. Distinguished guest, speakers, ladies and gentlemen, In view of the fact that harmonization of operations and standardization of infrastructures for payment and settlement systems are important for achieving a truly integrated markets in the region, I hope that all of us here could share valuable 3 / 4 thoughts and inputs through this business forum which will be beneficial for the development and re-shaping of Indonesian market infrastructures. These are not only to make the infrastructures and their operations more secure, robust and efficient but also to make them ready to support the implementation of ASEAN economic community (AEC) by 2015. Before I conclude, I would like to add some points of hard lessons learned from the most recent catastrophe which, I strongly believe have also to be integrated into the financial infrastructure we discuss today. First, we have to ensure that the financial market transaction should be closely linked with the underlying of real economic activities. Second, the financial infrastructure integration means involving a different law system, as well as business convention. Thus, it is important to also have sort of standardized financial market transaction, in particular the one that involve both cash and securities exchange to avoid possible dispute and arbitrage. Third, from what we observe in the US and Europe financial market in the aftermath of the crisis, it is increasingly important to adopt a more convergence accounting standard and increase transparency. In particular with regard the over-the-counter financial market transaction and financial institution balance sheet. Finally, I would like to express my gratitude to SWIFT for arranging such a beneficial business forum, as well as to the guest speakers for sharing their valuable thought in the next sessions. I truly hope that we are here today to have a better foundation for the better future. Thank you. Jakarta, 11 May 2010 4 / 4

Title: Remarks of the Deputy of Bank Indonesia on the inauguration of Bank Indonesia National Clearing System in the Clearing Regions of Palembang, Bengkulu, Bandarlampung, Palanglaraya, Jambi and LhokSeumawe Palembang, 1st March 2007
text: Remarks of the Deputy of Bank Indonesia on the inauguration of Bank Indonesia National Clearing System in the Clearing Regions of Palembang, Bengkulu, Bandarlampung, Palanglaraya, Jambi and LhokSeumawe Palembang, 1st March 2007 Governor of South Sumatera, Heads of banks, Ladies and Gentlemen, Assalamualaikum Warahmatullahi Wabarakatuh Good morning, I would like to take this opportunity to ask you all to praise the Lord God Almighty for his blessings that we can gather for the inauguration of Bank Indonesia National Clearing System in the Palembang, Bengkulu, Bandarlampung, Palangkaraya, Jambi and Lhok Seumawe branch office regions. Adoption in these regions represents the concluding phase of implementation in connection with the National Clearing System network. Subsequent to implementation in these regions, 96% of clearing transactions at the national level will have been integrated into the national clearing network. Currently, the transaction value processed through the network nationally is Rp4.5 trillion per day. The six regions we are celebrating today account for Rp189.7 billion per day through 7,916 transactions. Honorable ladies and gentlemen, The rapid expansion of technological innovation within the payment system has succeeded in changing the payment method from cash-based to non-cash. More specifically, the mode of payment is no longer paper-based but has evolved into paperless and electronic formats. The development of Bank Indonesias National Clearing System (SKNBI) is one such technological innovation designed and instituted to raise efficiency, improve reliability and ensure safety in the payment system. Efficiency gains primarily stem from cost cutting related to printing costs and paper handling, as well as more expeditious fund transfers. The previous fund settlement process, which was a manual process, took approximately two days (H2) or more, however with the National Clearing System fully on-line, transactions can be processed the same day. Furthermore, the National Clearing System can reduce the clearing position calculation of participants in each region. Just imagine if participants joined the clearing system from all clearing regions, which currently number about 106, this would mean that the National Clearing System would have to settle the clearing position in all 106 regions. Inefficiency occurred when participants were obliged to monitor all positions in all clearing regions. This implies sub-optimal liquidity management. With the National Clearing System, however, such inefficiency is eliminated as the clearing position of each participant will automatically be integrated nationally. Therefore, each participant will only have one clearing position per day. From another perspective, the real-time transmission of capital flows through the National Clearing System will accelerate the velocity of money, which can stimulate the public economy and, consequently, boost economic growth. The efficiency provided by the clearing system in the form of lower overheads and faster transaction processing will not only benefit banks but also the business community as well as the general public. In addition, the National Clearing System also facilitates prompt and accurate settlement, which offers assurance for transactions and minimizes the risk of default. Ladies and gentlemen, Through the application of Bank Indonesias National Clearing System, the various methods of clearing currently available can gradually be integrated into one national clearing system. With such a system, citizens in districts and subdistricts classified as remote areas can transfer funds through the clearing system providing the internal system of the participating bank is already on-line. It is expected that by the end of 2007, all non-BI clearing operators will adopt the BI National Clearing System. Distinguished guests, Bank Indonesia fully understands the dominant contribution of payment system transactions in supporting the sustainability of the national economy. To illustrate the point, the daily inter-bank transaction settlement value processed through the Real-time Gross Settle (RTGS) system is Rp118.2 trillion, meanwhile that settled through the clearing system is Rp4.7 trillion. This daily value is very significant since it represents about 1/5 (one-fifth) of the 2006 State Budget. It is not surprising that the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) recommended policies and a payment system that always adhere to international standards as written in the Core Principles on the Systemically Important Payment System. Compliance is essential as the magnitude of potential payment system risk is great, be it operational, human error, an unstable communications system or failed support infrastructure. Ladies and Gentlemen, Before I close, I would like to emphasize that the success of this implementation is not only the success of Bank Indonesia but also the success of all of us together through support, suggestions and participation to improve payment system efficiency. The success of clearing system implementation so far evidences our commitment and integrity. I would also like to take this opportunity to invite all banking officials and related stakeholders to support the success of Bank Indonesias National Clearing System. Allow me on behalf of the Board of Governors to thank you all for your participation in the implementation of the National Clearing System. Last but not least, by saying Bismillahirrohmanirrohiim, I would like to declare the Bank Indonesia National Clearing System, in Palembang, Bengkulu, Bandarlampung, Palangkaraya, Jambi and Lhok Seumawe, officially open. Thank you. Wassalamualaikum Wr. Wb. Palembang, 1st March 2007 Deputy Governor BANK INDONESIA Budi Rochadi 6

Title: Keynote Speech by Deputy Governor, Budi Mulya at Indonesian Bankers Association Summit
text: OUTLOOK OF THE INDONESIAN BANKING INDUSTRY AMIDST THE GLOBAL FINANCIAL CRISIS1 BUDI MULYA Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia Members of Indonesian Bankers Association; Ladies and Gentlemen, Assalamualaikum wr. Wb. First and foremost, I would like to extend my gratitude for this invitation to speak at such an illustrious forum of the Indonesian Bankers Association here this evening, representing Dr. Boediono  the Governor of Bank Indonesia. It is a great opportunity for us all to meet at the outset of this new year. The year 2009 is set to be replete with onerous challenges corresponding to the changing dynamics occurring in the global financial market and economy. We all survived 2008, a time that will be hard for us to forget. We have all seen, bared witness and felt the sheer magnitude and widespread effects of the financial market shocks; one of the biggest in history, especially following the collapse of one of the US largest financial institutions  Lehman Brothers Holding Inc on 15th September 2008. We should all heed the lessons from this very expensive experience, in particular to ensure that the Indonesian banking industry, which also suffered a crisis in the last decade, can become more seasoned, more durable and more optimal in its role for the Indonesian economy. During this year of 2009, the professionalism of all of us, both the authorities and business players alike, especially in the banking industry, will be beset with arduous challenges in the midst of escalating uncertainty, which entails 1 Speech delivered at Indonesian Bankers Association Summit, Jakarta 25th February 2009 rising risk. We must all maintain our optimism while remaining realistic so that we can be ready to face and overcome the worst, however unexpected it may be Ladies and Gentlemen, Allow me to open my speech here this evening by briefly illustrating how the global financial crisis is far worse than initially expected. The effects of the global financial crisis are now felt deeper and wider than first projected, and any signs of recovery are yet to emerge. Some analysts/experts have even gone as far as stating that if the negative effects on the global economy reach their nadir in 2009, then we should consider ourselves very lucky. This is seen from the perspective of an escalating recession threat, rising unemployment and a dearth of capital flows to the real sector. Global economic growth has experienced a very significant correction, greater than initially thought. In its most recent projection2, the IMF predicted that the global economy would only grow by 0.5% from the previously expected 2.2%. Economic growth in the US, Europe and Japan will even suffer a contraction (negative growth) exceeding initial projections. They will respectively grow by minus 1.6%, minus 2.0% and minus 2.6%. Meanwhile, the global trade volume is expected to experience a larger contraction than initial projections, namely minus 4.8%. This, of course, will have bigger and wider consequences for other countries around the globe because of a subsequent drop in demand for goods and services worldwide. A similar picture can also be seen in the Asian region. China, who was widely expected to be a pillar of global growth amidst the crisis, is also expected to suffer a significant slowdown. According to the Consensus Forecast, in 2009 China is expected to only grow by 7% - worlds away from previous double-digit growth. The same is true for India, which is expected to only grow by 5.1% from initial projections of 6.3%. Some 2 IMF, World Economic Outlook, update 28th January 2009 countries with a high dependence on exports, such as South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore, may even suffer negative growth. Meanwhile, the Indonesian economy is also expected to experience a significant correction. Looking at the deteriorating global economic outlook the downside risk of Indonesian economic growth will remain large. The Consensus Forecast, for example, predicts that the Indonesian economy will only grow by 3.9% at the end of 2009. Conversely, inflation is no longer a dominant issue due to the declination of commodity and energy prices on the back of weaker global aggregate demand. Inflation in 2009 is expected to decline into the range of 5% - 7%. Addressing such a monumental global economic threat, the response of the fiscal authority and central bank in various countries has also been extraordinary yet comprehensive. Numerous large-scale stimulus packages have been implemented, including bank recapitalization like we experienced 11 years ago. We also see how coordination among authorities, as in the Chiang Mai Initiative (Asean plus 3), in various countries improved to overcome or minimize the crisis effects as well as to accelerate recovery despite its protracted process. This crisis also further strengthened re-regulation of the global financial market. Recommendations on this have been issued by the Group of Thirty (G30) at the Financial Reform: A Framework for Financial Stability published on 15th January 2009. G30 members include economic experts and policymakers as well as prominent former policymakers, headed by Paul Volker (former Chairman of Board of Governors of The Fed) and include Tim Geithner (current US Finance Minister), Larry Summer (former Treasury and current economic advisor to President Barack Obama) and Jean-Claude Trichet (the President of European Central Bank). Ladies and Gentlemen, The immense losses suffered by global banks and financial institutions, further exacerbated by deteriorating economies in some countries, have increased global risk perception. Some countries in Eastern Europe such as the Ukraine, Latvia, Hungary and Belarus, as well as Pakistan in Asia and Iceland were forced to seek IMF support. Widespread uncertainty, risk aversion and flight to quality have caused the rise in risk perception in developed countries to propagate wildly. One indicator of the rise in this risk perception can be seen from credit default swaps (CDS) that again jumped at the beginning of 2009, showing a similar pattern in developing countries, including Indonesia. CDS, which was initially a financial market product to hedge corporate default risk, is now being used for risk related to sovereign debt. Amidst the sharp decline in global interest rates, even approaching zero in some developed countries, coupled with burgeoning global budget deficits, there is a high probability that CDS will become the indicator most widely used by market players to gauge the exchange rate direction of a country. The behavior of market players in the financial market, more specifically easily panicked and the widespread phenomenon of flight to quality, has also compounded pressures on global exchange rates towards the US Dollar. Global exchange rates weakened and have become more volatile. In Asia, the Korean Won for instance, has suffered significant depreciation of 14.84% since the beginning of 2009. The Rupiah has depreciated by 9.02% in 2009. A similarly gloomy picture has emerged on the stock markets too. Global stock indices experienced significant pressures because, amidst the deteriorating global economy, investors tended to divert their funds to Treasury bonds (especially US T-Bills) or gold. In the Asian region, the stock index in Vietnam has plummeted 19.25% in 2009, whereas the indices in Hong Kong (Hang Seng) dropped by 9.48%, Singapore (STI) by 7.51% and our IHSG 2.34% compared to the beginning of 2009. Ladies and Gentlemen, In response to the exchange rate pressures I have mentioned, Bank Indonesia persevered in trying to maintain the exchange rate and avoid excessive fluctuations, however, as part of the free-floating exchange rate system that we chose to adopt, BI cannot endeavor to maintain a particular level. This is crucial considering that excessive volatility would aggravate uncertainty for business players and further invite unwanted speculative action. In the midst of rising foreign exchange demand, especially US Dollar, and high counterparty risk between market players, Bank Indonesia introduced operational policy to aid the distribution and balance of foreign exchange liquidity requirement through US Dollar Repo instruments with Global Bonds (Foreign Exchange SUN) collateral and USD/Rupiah swap transactions. The effects of the global financial crisis, especially risk aversion and flight to quality, also undermined the price of treasury bonds (SUN) so that SUN yield rebounded at the beginning of the year for all tenures. On average, SUN yield has experienced a rise of 200 bps since the beginning of the year, especially for tenures of over 10 years. SUN yield increased due to the current declination in interest rates and strong external factors, especially related to the increase in risk perception. Meanwhile, the inter-bank money market in Indonesia has continued to function well. Inter-bank liquidity is yet to flow optimally because of increasing segmentation corresponding to rising counterparty risk between banks. The ongoing phenomenon in the global financial market is that liquidity flows in the money market nearly ground to a halt amid the hoarding of liquidity. Some would argue that the recovery of the global money market will still take a very long time. Alan Greenspan, former Governor of US Central Bank for example, as reported by Bloomberg on 23rd February 2009 opined that the global money market would recover, at the earliest, in 2010. This is further evidenced by the spread between the 3-month LIBOR and OIS that is still high at above 1%. Similar indications have also been seen in the domestic money market. The spread between JIBOR  OIS and JIBOR with non-overnight tenure with overnight JIBOR, which despite starting to narrow is still far higher compared to normal conditions. This, of course, indicates that banks still prefer to place their excess funds in Bank Indonesia rather than loan to other banks, as seen by the position of BI open market operations, including fine-tune contraction (FTC) that has tended to increase, while inter-bank transaction volume has declined. Considering that it is crucial to maintain the function of the inter-bank money market, Bank Indonesia has taken a number of measures necessary to help liquidity flow in the inter-bank money market. These include activating repo purchase transactions for bonds (SBI/SUN) in FTE and repo to 14 days. This 14-day repo transaction is available daily. However, this clearly would not be optimal if not supported by the banks themselves because the root of the problem is not the absence of liquidity in the market but more a factor of risk perception so that liquidity does not flow. For that, in the future banks are expected to have a healthier portfolio asset composition, especially in maintaining a certain amount of liquid assets in their portfolio. In this respect, Bank Indonesia has promoted such issues by implementing a kind of liquidity ratio as part of the banking minimum reserve requirement, which will come into effect in October 2009. Ladies and Gentlemen, What I have outlined so far here this evening serves as an illustration of the current circumstances faced by our banking industry. Despite these formidable challenges, the role of banks must remain optimal with greater prudence to tackle future pressures and challenges. So far we can say that our banking conditions are sound. In relation to the current global financial crisis, it can be said that our banking practices are still relatively conventional, particularly in terms of relying on public deposits to fund credit (very low money market leverage) and the relatively tenuous relations with global financial market products, but this is a blessing in disguise. However, in the future this will certainly entail its own risks among growing alternative investment products, especially for large depositors. For that, banks still need to seek innovative breakthroughs to strengthen their funding base in a measurable and transparent manner. Some of the latest indicators still demonstrate relatively sound Indonesian banking conditions. Industry CAR is still 16.2% on average, NPL is still manageable at 3.8% (gross) and the return on assets (ROA) is high (2.3%) as per December 2008. However, in terms of capital, under current circumstances higher capital for each individual bank would be far better. With the declining interest rate, bank interest rates including term deposits and credit have also started to come down, although this is still relatively slow and not as expected. From the liquidity side, it is not a healthy competitive practice in the industry should banks compete through a term deposit interest rate war when it comes to funding aspects. Breakthroughs are required as I previously stated to strengthen the resilience of bank funds. In this respect, instruments such as inter-bank syndication loans are probably necessary to be reviewed as alternative. Ladies and Gentlemen, With the development of future economic conditions that will continue to decelerate, bank credit growth for all economic types and sectors will also suffer a decline. Working capital credit and the industrial sector have shown the largest slowdowns since the end of 2008. This is obviously an acceptable consequence of developments in the real sector. Frankly speaking, the 30% credit growth achieved in 2008 is not going to happen in 2009. This year, credit growth is expected to slow to around 15.5%. However, a variety of risks need to be monitored and anticipated, in particular the potential of increasing non-performing loans, which may lead to a drop in bank ROA and CAR. Growth in public deposits, which to this date is the primary source of bank placement funding, is expected to grow negatively. As I have discussed already this evening, considering the dominant role of banks in the economy, bank intermediation must continue to be optimal in the future. With reference to credit extension, loans to the MSME sector, which is proven to have resilience against the crisis, need to be accelerated. This is in itself a form of spreading bank fund placement risk. Meanwhile, Bank Indonesia together with the Government will keep improving policy coordination to ensure the establishment of propitious conditions for banks and the economy in general in order to catalyze economic growth and prevent it dropping below some of the more pessimistic forecasts. In this respect, macroeconomic and financial market stability will be the overarching priority. In the banking field, regulations will be directed towards providing bank flexibility in the extension of credit, but coupled with better governance and risk management. Bank Indonesia will also persist with improving the quality of bank supervision in order to maintain the role of banks in the economy and so that the bitter experiences of the 1997/98 crisis do not reoccur. At this opportunity, I would like to ask all of you to strive to improve our professionalism, particularly in measuring and addressing risk so that Indonesian banks can advance with better resilience. With good intentions and honest behavior in the pursuit of normal profits, God willing, we will all emerge on the other side of these troubling times prepared to confront whatever challenges we may face. Hopefully, all you Indonesian bankers can contribute optimally to the national economy. Billahi taufiq wal hidayah wassalamualaikum wa Rahmatullah wa Barakatuh Jakarta 25th February 2009

Title: 14th Meeting of Standing Committee on Assessment of Vulnerabilities (SCAV) Sydney, 25 February 2014 Remarks by Dr. Halim Alamsyah, Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia
text: 14th Meeting of Standing Committee on Assessment of Vulnerabilities (SCAV) Sydney, 25 February 2014 Remarks by Dr. Halim Alamsyah, Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia Distinguished members of the Committee, It is both a pleasure and an honor for me to have the opportunity delivering my views on how the Emerging Markets (EMs) meet and respond to the current economic challenges. Last year was indeed a very challenging time for Emerging Markets (EMs). Home grown challenges have been compounded by the subsequent period of volatility in international financial market when market expectations over-reacted toward the scaling back of Unconventional Monetary Polices (UMP) by the US-Fed. Amidst heightened uncertainty and risk aversion globally, concerns about the sustainability of external positions in some EMs also came to the fore. And this has plagued countries such as Brazil, Indonesia, India, Turkey, and South Africa, and has amplified capital outflows from EMs to a varying degree, according to their perceived vulnerabilities. This has led to significant re- pricing of EM assets, thus putting enormous pressures on the EMs financial markets as bond yield rose, equity price dropped, CDS increased sharply, and exchange rate depreciated markedly. Individually, authorities in each EM have responded in tackling these challenges. Most EMs, including Indonesia, have resorted to rather conventional policy responses such as tight monetary policy eventhough with varying degree and timing, more flexible exchange rate movements, as well as fiscal reforms to strengthen public finances and ensure fiscal sustainability. Some EMs has also taken structural reforms in several areas in order to control the widening current account deficits and to regains economic growth momentum. Whenever the situation permits, especially politically, some EMs including Indonesia also step up the implementation of preventive measures through macroprudential policy to address risks related to the property market and household indebtedness. Ladies and Gentlemen, Given the policy responses and the cautious optimism on global economic recovery ahead, it remains to be seen whether the EMs have really yet out of the trouble. Some vulnerabilities remains in many EMs. One source of vulnerability in Emerging Markets that should be addressed is current account deficit that remains sizeable in some countries. To correct this problem definitely will need more than just tight monetary and exchange rate policies. It surely needs a much broader structural policy responses and consistency in its implementation. Another source of vulnerability relates to a high short term foreign ownership both in equity and fixed income markets. The consequences of these flows which are easily moves in and out the country that has a relatively shallow financial market have proved to be able to create dramatic volatility in the capital and foreign exchange 1 market. Adding to the vulnerability is an indication of increasing private external debts, particularly in non-financial companies in many EMs. Some emerging markets have been indicated by the BIS to have large issuance of corporate international bonds. As we have seen currently, an abrupt rise in risk aversion might pressure the sharp increase in their yields. The downside risk to countries would heighten in those vulnerable Emerging Markets, should the Fed's policy rate rise earlier or higher than expected and pass through the effects to both trade and financial channels. One thing we can note however that most of the banking/financial sector in EMs generally have strong capital and liquidity positions; This is no coincidence, but it is a result of EMs commitment to implement the international agreed financial system reform. With a relatively strong banking condition, the financial sector in many EMs, including Indonesia, has been able to deal with excessive turbulences coming from external origins. Members of the Committee, Let me turn now to the experience of Indonesia. I will briely describe our recent developments together with some vulnerabilities and policy responses that have been taken to address the issues. Since the last 5 years, Indonesian economy has been growing at about 5.8% p.a. with inflation averages around 5.2% p.a. and the exchange rate tends to strengthen from above Rpll,000/US in 2009 to below Rp9,000/US in 2011, before weakening since 2012. Fiscal deficits also remains moderate with an average of -1.5% p.a. Current account position recorded a surplus during the last 5 years with foreign exchange reserves accelerated from US66 billion to as high as US124,6 billion in August 2011, before declining since early 2012. Total external debt of private sector reached US140.5 billion or 16% of GDP at the end of 2013, and it comprised 29% short term debt (below 1 year) and 71% long term debt. Some of private external debt came from related parties such as parent company 23% and other afiliated parties 9%. Eventhough private external debt slightly increased compare to 2009 which is recorded 14% of GDP, it remains manageable. The problems begin to emerge when the slow down in global economy and commodity prices eventually started to weaken Indonesia's exports. The decline of exports at the time when imports are rising due to strong domestic demand has worsened the trade balance and turned the current account into deficit since the end of 2012, reaching the worst deficit of 4.4% of GDP in Q2-2013. Fiscal deficits remained moderate to around 2% in 2012-2013 due to conservative fiscal stance. Nevertheless, demand for subsidized fuels was behind most of those deficits both in the state budget and current account, prompting the Government to increase domestic fuel price in June 2013 although by moderately. The situation was getting more serius as US-Fed tapering off was announced in May 2013. With current account (also trade balance) in deficits and inflation rising as a consequence of fuel price hike, Indonesia began to see sizeable capital reversals especially from portfolio investments both in the forms of fixed income and equity, giving considerable pressures on the exchange rate. With lack of dollar supply and shallow 2 domestic forex market. Bank Indonesia had to intervene just to contain excessive volatilies in the market. Eventually, coupled with several policy responses including policy rate increases of 175 bps, Bank Indonesia did managed to contain the depreciation of the currency. Rupiah exchange rate depreciation reached around 26% y.o.y in 2013, making it the worst currency performance in EMEs. Consequently, FX reserves declined significantly touching US95.1 billion at end September 2013, before gradually increasing again recently to US101 billion in January 2014. It worth noted that the banking sector in Indonesia has sufficient cushions, ensuring that the sector is less susceptible to external shocks. Banks are supported by strong capital (CAR) of above 18% p.a, and ample liquidity with NPL of less than 2% (in gross terms). Clearly, the results of years of improvement in banking regulations and supervision as well as stronger risk management and corporate governance since the Asian Crisis has made the banks are now well managed, well capitalized, liquid and very profitable. Nonetheless, efforts remain to be done to improve banks' efficiency. Ladies and Gentlemen, In response to the current shifting of global economic landscape, Indonesia has moved to counterbalance the recent volatility by making macro-economic stability a top policy priority. Policies that focus on stability over growth have been put in place to prepare Indonesia for a soft landing. The policy mix designed for a soft landing mode of the economy has clearly directed toward anchoring inflation to the targeted range, reducing current account deficit toward sustainable level, and strengthening the financial system stability. Central bank interest rate response (175 bps interest rate increase) was combined with the more flexible exchange rate, financial market deepening, and macroprudential measures. The Government also took a number of structural reforms in the area of fiscal, investment, and energy sectors. Such a policy mix and close policy coordination between the Central Bank and the Government have been able to stabilize the macroeconomic and financial condition, bringing the economy to soft landing in 2013, thus provide a better ground for further improvement in 2014. Economic growth declined moderately from 6.23% in 2012 to 5.78% in 2013. With the bold measures from the central bank monetary policy and prompt response from the government, the pressures to the inflation were short lived and well contained, bringing down the inflation from the hike in 2013 that reached above 8.4%. We expect the inflation rate will be able to meet its target range of 4.5% 1% in 2014. Policy responses by Indonesian authorities have also left favorable impact on the Balance of Payments (BoP). After three quarters of deficit, BoP recently returned to positive territory by posting US4.4 billion surpluses in Q4-2013, contributed by falling deficit in current account and increased surplus in capital account. Narrowing current account deficit from 4.4% of GDP in Q2-2013 to 2% of GDP in Q4 2013 is on the account of rising demand from Advanced Economies, moderated domestic demand, and favorable exchange rate. Exchange rate flexibility helps as adjustment mechanism for lowering 3 current account deficit. Meanwhile, foreign capital flows have also surged in again. This BoP development subsequently resulted in the rise of international reserves, return its position into above US100 billion equivalent to 5.7 months of import and official debt repayment. In line with improved fundamental, pressures on Rupiah exchange rate have receded recently. After having depreciated more than 20% in 2013, currently the exchange rate is stays at around Rpll,800/US, strengthened from Rpl2,189/US by end of December 2013. We realized that we should be remained vigilant on the persisting source of vulnerability. The existing shallow domestic foreign exchange market causes the rupiah exchange rate easily to overshoot and suffers from high volatility. Adding to this source of vulnerability is the increasing in the private external debts, particularly in non-financial corporations (NFCs). Those external debts, if not well managed, may potentially cause difficulties for the corporations, should there be a sudden shock in the exchange rate. Moreover, the large portion of foreign holding on equities in the stock market, government securities, and Bank Indonesia instruments, which mostly in short term tenor, make our financial account are susceptible to sudden capital outflows that may cause shortage of foreign exchange supply in the domestic market, heighten pressures to the rupiah exchange rate. On the banking sector, liquidity risk increased our attention lately, as the appetite for banks to over-expand in lending activities persists in some banks, while their sources of funding are limited.
