Inappropriate manner and unnecessary financial engineering could be minimized since the financial activities will be conducted based on Islamic fundamental elements that prioritize justice and fairness, sustainability, and inclusion. In addition, the equity based financial transaction could reduce formidable dependence to debt funding and therefore the risks arise from the excessive external borrowing could be mitigated. 17. Another key feature of Islamic finance is the capability to promote wealth distribution. Studies have shown that many people in OIC member countries still live under poverty line and are unable to transform themselves into part of productive society due to the lack of assets in hand and the absence of financial products and services with low cost of funds. In this context, zakat and awqaf program should be further optimized to enhance wealth distribution among society. 18. In the context of zakat and awqaf, Indonesia has huge potential. The zakat potential is estimated to be around USD22.6 billion or equivalent to 3.4% of Indonesias Gross Domestic Product in 20111. Nevertheless, the collected zakat is far from optimum level, i.e. only 1.2% of the zakat potential. Meanwhile, the market value of registered lands awqaf in Indonesia is about USD60 billion. The effective optimization of those lands will provide significant amount of funds to support poverty alleviation program. 1 Source: Islamic Finance Social Report 2014 6 Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, 19. Before I conclude my remarks, I would like to underline that it is undeniable that Islamic finance offers a new equilibrium that will contribute to promote sustainable economic growth and financial stability. An intriguing issue is how the authorities establish framework to maintain the Islamic finance stability. 20. From the central banks point of view, the stability of Islamic financial system is very important for two reasons. First, Islamic financial system could serve as the other pillar to sustain the national development program, particularly with the characteristics that are pro-growth, pro-employment, and pro-stability. Second, with the growing presence of the industry, potential adverse impact resulted from the failures in the Islamic financial system may become more severe if it is poorly managed. 21. A number of steps have been initiated through the implementation of micro-prudential and macro-prudential regulations, policy instruments and supporting infrastructure. The presence of lenderof-the-last-resort facility that allows the central bank to provide solvent but illiquid Islamic banks is one of the examples to maintain the operational soundness high. 22. Finally, please allow me to wish you all a fruitful discussion and deliberation in this important event. I am sure that supported by internationally reputable academics and players, we can achieve significant outcomes that are beneficial to promote development in this particular area. I wish this program a great success. Thank you. Wassalamualaykum warahmatullah wabarakatuh. 7

Title: Keynote Speech by Halim Alamsyah Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia in Forum on Product Innovations for Financial Inclusion: Promoting Payment and Banking Product Innovations for Expanding Access to Finance" Jakarta, 13 November 2013
text: BANK INDONESIA Keynote Speech Mr. Halim Alamsyah At the Event FORUM ON PRODUCT INNOVATIONS FOR FINANCIAL INCLUSION: PROMOTING PAYMENT AND BANKING PRODUCT INNOVATIONS FOR EXPANDING ACCESS TO FINANCE Jakarta, 13 November 2013 Honorable,  Representatives of Fiscal Policy Agency (BKF),  Representatives of Financial Services Authority (OJK),  Representatives of Team of Poverty Alleviation Acceleration National (TNP2K),  Country Manager International Finance Corporation (IFC) and World Bank;  Fellow Speakers; and  Distinguished Guests Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh, Good Morning and Greetings to us all, There are no other words that we can say this morning except to praise our gratitude to Allah SWT, God the Almighty, for His grace we gather here in healthy condition and excellence atmosphere at the Forum on Product Innovations for Financial Inclusion with the following theme Promoting Payment and Banking Product Innovations for Expanding Access to Finance. This forum is jointly organized by Bank Indonesia with IFC and World Bank, supported by BKF (Fiscal Policy Agency, of the Ministry of Finance), OJK (Financial Services Authority) and TNP2K (Team of Poverty Alleviation Acceleration National), as the ministry and institution associated with inclusive financial program. -- Ladies and Gentlemen, As the survey result on household balance conducted by Bank Indonesia in 2012, only 48% of the total households in Indonesia possessed savings accounts in banks, non-bank financial institutions, and non-financial institutions. In other words there are 52% households in Indonesia that did not have savings at all. This is parallel with the World Bank Survey in 2010 stating that in Indonesia, access to formal financial services was only available for half of Indonesias population. Around 32% of the population even did not have savings (both in formal and informal sector), and included in the category of financially excluded. From the perspective of financial literacy, the result of Bank Indonesia survey year 2006 provided a conclusion that increase of knowledge on finance and banking for the majority of Indonesias society was still required. Similarly with the result of the World Bank survey in 2010, stating that one of the main challenges of the low demand from the community for financial services was the ignorance of the community about financial products and services. Such condition has convinced Bank Indonesia that Financial Inclusion policy is required and such policy needs to be implemented nationally, namely engaging some ministries and institutions in order to acquire an optimal result. Therefore, the existence of National Strategy of Inclusive Finance and National Coordinator of Inclusive Finance become very important to be possessed by Indonesia. Distinguish Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, In the National Strategy of Inclusive Finance already launched by the Government in June 2012, financial inclusion or inclusive finance is defined as a Comprehensive activities intended to eliminate all forms of barriers both price and non-price in nature, toward access of the community to utilize financial services. Various activities in the context of financial inclusion are intended to achieve the vision of To realize the widest access of community to the financial services easily in order to support a quality economic growth to enhance the peoples welfare. Ladies and Gentlemen, Distinguished Guests, To achieve the vision of inclusive financial policy, six pillars of inclusive financial activities have been formulated as well as the main products that will be the objects in the inclusive financial activities. The six main activities as the pillars of inclusive financial police are: (1) Financial Education; (2) Public Financial Facility; (3) Mapping of financial information; (4) Supporting Regulation; (5) Facilitation of Intermediation and Distribution Channel; and (6) Customer Protection. Whereas the respective pillar will have various activities to realize inclusive finance. Meanwhile, main financial products that will be the objects in inclusive financial policy are savings, credit/financing, paying system, insurance related to credit, and also other financial products and services for MSME. Ladies and Gentlemen, Various activities have been conducted by Bank Indonesia and also the relevant ministries and institutions in order to support inclusive finance. Just mention the financial education intensively conducted by Bank Indonesia and OJK; efforts in increasing availability and utilization of TabunganKu (My Savings) by Bank Indonesia and the banking industry; and program of Government assistance distribution through banking (G2P  Government to Person) by Bank Indonesia and the Ministries. From all the programs implemented, it cannot be denied that the roles of financial product innovation and technology development as well as information hold the primary roles. Therefore, efforts to encourage various product innovation are required that will ease and expedite the community, specifically the unbanked, under-banked and MSME, to connect with financial services. Ladies and Gentlemen, Distinguished Guests, Currently, banking products and also paying system using the facility of technology and information are already developed, such as e-commerce, mobile banking, and product innovation linking virtual payment with credit provision, liquidity management and insurance. Media used is not limited to banks, but also engaging other financial service providers such as telecommunication companies. Not only that, development of some programs is also currently being conducted in order to minimize asymmetric information between the community namely the unbanked people and MSME with Banking among others for assessment of credit rating development. Further step is to attempt that the innovation conducted can achieve inclusive financial vision, so that it requires efforts to coach and mentoring, i.e. to educate the community on financial management and utilization of technology. In this case development and utilization of technology require behavior change of the society who originally used to take the traditional way. Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, In the future, it is expected that innovation of technology and information can support the development of payment facilities and banking products to increase financial access of the community particularly the unbanked, under-banked and MSME. Therefore, I expect that this forum can be the event for exchanging information on international practices and also for discussions and exchanging ideas between the policy makers and private sectors which resolutions will further encourage financial product innovation in the context of Inclusive Financial Policy. In this opportunity also, I would like to express my appreciation and thanks to the relevant Ministries and institutions, IFC and the World Bank on the organizing of this event. Finally, may all our efforts in the development of this nation be blessed by Allah SWT. That is all for now and thank you. Wabillahitaufik walhidayah, Wassalamu alaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh. Jakarta, 13 November 2011

Title: Structural Reform for Sustainable Economic Growth (Keynote Speech by Agus D.W Martowardojo Governor of Bank Indonesia at Discussion and Book Launching of Indonesias Economic Report (LPI) 2013) Jakarta, 2 April 2014
text: Keynote Speech Governor of Bank Indonesia Structural Reform for Sustainable Economic Growth Discussion and Book Launching of Indonesias Economic Report (LPI) 2013 Jakarta, 2 April 2014 Honorable,  Former Governors of Bank Indonesia,  Members of DPR RI,  Speakers and Moderator,  Members of BSBI  Members of Board Governors of Bank of Indonesia, and  Ladies and Gentlemen, Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh, Good afternoon and greetings to us all, 1. First of all, please allow me to ask you all to praise the God Almighty, for His grace and blessing we gather here attending the Book Launching of Indonesias Economy Report (LPI) 2013, and to be followed by a discussion with a topic on Structural Reform for Sustainable Economic. 2. This LPI book is an annual routine publication of Bank Indonesia since long. Besides explaining various dynamics of Indonesias economy in the relevant year, including policy responses conducted, LPI also seeks to convey lessons learned. The efforts to dig from the lessons of the economic trip are fairly important as it can become the foundation for the strengthening of policy in enhancing economic resilience of Indonesia in years to come. Ladies and Gentlemen, 3. In LPI 2013, as it has been conveyed frequently in various occasions, Indonesias economy of 2013 faced challenges that were not easy. The global financial market encountered risk-off when the Fed giving a signal for tapering. In June 2013 alone outflow of portfolio capital occurred has reached 4.1 billion. Amidst the support of the not fairly strong domestic economic structure, such global strain gave a heavy pressure to our economy, at least up to QIII2013. 4. Behind the various dynamic and challenges of the 2013 economy, we see some important lessons that emerged, namely lessons related to policies that need to be taken to maintain the continuity of economic growth in the future. 5. First lesson is related to the importance of maintaining discipline and commitment to macro-economic policy, both fiscal and monetary, in directing economy to the more sustainable growth. 6. In this aspect, pre-emptive and bold monetary policy undertook by Bank Indonesia in 2013 has provided an anchor to the controlled inflation expectation and also directed the current account balance to the level that was more healthy. Similarly, the fiscal policy that consistently maintained its sustainability was able to manage the economy controlled, and to support the efforts to strengthen the resilience of Indonesias balance of payments. 7. Second lesson is the strategic of policy integration and interaction in response to the increasing complexity of the challenges. Response of policy cannot rely to one instrument only, but it needs to be supported and strengthened by other instruments. 8. Integration in the context of interaction of monetary policy and fiscal policy needs to be strengthened as well, so that policy effectiveness becomes more optimal. Aside from that, policy integration is also intended to respond not only to short term issues and cyclical, but also needs to be directed to overcome medium term and structural problems. 9. Third lesson is the importance of financial system resilience to support economic adjustment to remain under control. We should be grateful that amidst the strong pressure toward domestic economy, financial system stability in Indonesia in year 2013 remained under control. Ladies and Gentlemen, 10. Response to policy that was pre-emptive and bold conducted by Bank Indonesia and the Government, in general has directed our economy to stable again and started to move to a more balanced direction. As we all observe, in Q IV-2013 the current account deficit started to decline to a more healthy level supported by the economic stability that was controlled again. 11. Although the response of monetary policy taken was quite bold, and yet with a measured pace so that the national economy was prevented from hard landing. Indonesias economic growth in 2013 could be maintained at 5.8%, higher if compared to the economic growth of the peer countries. 12. In our opinion, other than macro condition that started to become stable and balanced, the structure of financial micro market also began to show direction that further improving, especially in the foreign exchange market. Liquidity of foreign exchange is flowing more smoothly in inter-banks markets and the formed conversion rate is healthier. 13. The improving condition of macro-economy and micro market has reinforced the trust of global investors. This is reflected by the large inflow of portfolio capital in the last three month of 2014 that reached Rp54 trillion and rupiah that was appreciated at 7.0%. In the last issuance of 22 February, the Economist magazine also considered Indonesia should be out from the fragile five; the combination of higher rates and a cheaper currency nurtured a rebalancing. Indonesia no longer looks so fragile. 14. With that achievement, we are optimistic that economic growth in 2014 will be maintained at range of 5.5%-5.9% followed by sources of growth that are more balanced. On other perspective, inflation is predicted to remain controlled in its target range of 4.5%1% and deficit of current account can be down below 3.0% toward GDP. Honorable Attendees, 15. Achievement and projection of economy that is improving certainly does not make us complacent. Behind the positive achievement, we must soonest conduct various improvement measures to face challenges in the years to come. 16. The said improvement measures are related to the last lesson emerged in 2013. The fourth lesson shall be related to the importance of structural reform that can enhance our industrial capability, so that it can motivate a stronger economic growth, and yet without followed by the increase of current balance deficit and increase of inflation pressure. We expect economic prospect in medium term can be higher if various structural constraints that hamper the increase of industrial capability can be overcome soon. 17. As it will be elaborated by Mr. Mirza Adityaswara in the discussion later on, we see three structural challenges that need to get immediate priority. First, real sector condition that still needs enhancement of competitiveness and reliability from the production perspective. Second, various basic capital of development such as physical and digital connectivity infrastructure, human resources and capacity of technological absorption, and business climate and institutional that still need to be strengthened. Finally, related to the financing of development, which remains not optimal as the impact of domestic financial market that is not deep yet. 18. In connection with this challenge, we believe that implementation of structural reform policy needs to be focused on the three main pillars, i.e. (a) strengthening of competitiveness of industrial sector, (b) self-reliant domestic economy, and (c) source of development financing that is continuous, both derived from external and domestic sources. 19. Certainly, the strengthening of the three pillars needs to be supported by policies to realize the resilience of energy and food as well as the strengthening of basic capital of development. 20. While further strengthening the disciplines of fiscal and monetary policies, the measure of structural reform acceleration can be divided into three sectors. First, enhancement of competitiveness and economic self-reliance through strengthening of production structure and integration into global value chain. Second, improve fiscal space in supporting economic growth through optimization of energy subsidies management. And third, strengthening the development financing through financial market deepening and creation of a favorable climate to encourage capital flow in the form of FDI. However, in our opinion, the inflow of FDI needs to be directed to export-based sectors so as not to raise pressure in the current account balance. 21. We believe that the three areas of policies are critical to be conducted. Indonesia as a middle-income country, cannot afford to only rely on cheap labor wages and extractive economic activities. On the contrary, our economy must move toward self-reliant economy supported by industrial-based innovation ecosystem. 22. In this regard, more solid attention from various parties is expected, so that the resulted policies are not stuck on a short term interest, but look into the nations interest in the long term. 23. We, in Bank Indonesia, determined to consistently support this structural reform. We believe there is no other choice for Indonesia but to perform it in order to avoid from the risk of middle income trap. Ladies and Gentlemen, 24. Before ending my speech, on behalf of the Board of Governors of Bank Indonesia allow us to present the Indonesias Economic Report 2013. We hope that this report may become a quality reference in preparing measures forward to strengthen economic structure amidst the transition season that is full of uncertainties. 25. Those efforts to strengthen the economic structure are in accordance with the cover picture of LPI 2013 book concerning the tradition of Fahombo, Hombo Batu, or skipping stones, in Nias community. This tradition we believe can be the proper symbolic reflection for our economy, namely the requirement of vision sharpness and strong resilience as well as maintained stability to overcome challenges, just likes the towering stones, and ability to have a soft landing, namely set foot back to the ground without. 26. We also would like express our gratitude to the speakers/resource persons and moderator who are willing to fulfill our invitation in this discussion concerning Structural Reform for Sustainable Economic Growth. We hope that the discussion will further strengthen our resolve to accelerate the structural reform in order to maintain the sustainable economic growth. 27. Finally, may Allah, God the Gracious and Merciful, blesses this activity and constantly give His counseling, guidance, and grace to us all in our work. Thank you. Wassalamu alaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh. Agus D.W. Martowardoyo Governor of Bank Indonesia

Title: Keynote Speech Halim Alamsyah Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia At The National Seminar on "Multiple-License Policy" Jakarta, 7 February 2013
text: KEYNOTE SPEECH DEPUTY GOVERNOR OF BANK INDONESIA AT THE NATIONAL SEMINAR ON MULTIPLE-LICENSE POLICY Jakarta, 7 February 2013 Bismillahir Rahmaannir Rahiim The Honorable,  Mr. Darmono, Deputy Attorney General of RI and a Member of IKA UUI Trustees that is willing to take time to open this seminar  Banking Leaders, Economists, Academicians and Representatives of Associations  Speakers and Moderators at the seminar this morning, Messrs. Irwan Lubis, Zulkifli Zaini, Mirza Adityaswara, Ryan Kiryanto and Madam Aviliani  Board of Management of IKA UII and ISEI Jakarta Branch  Distinguished Guests Assalamu alaikum Wr. Wb., Good Morning and Greetings to all. 1. To start this morning meeting, lets pray our gratitude and praise to Allah SWT, God the Almighty, for His blessings we gather here in a good condition to start this meeting and to follow the agenda of this National Seminar initiated by IKA UII and ISEI Jakarta Branch. For that reason, as the member of the Board of Governors of Bank Indonesia, I would like to extend my appreciation to the Board of Management of IKA UII and ISEI Jakarta Branch that has helped Bank Indonesia in socializing the multiple-license policy that will become the topic of todays seminar. Ladies and Gentlemen, Background of the issuance of Multi-license regulation 2. As it is already known, last 27 December 2012, Bank Indonesia has issued a BI Regulation (PBI) concerning Business Activities and Office Network Based on Bank Core Capital or frequently referred to as PBI Multi-license. The issuance of this regulation is intended to increase the resilience and competitiveness of national banking through banking structuring by overseeing business activities and opening office network adjusted with capacity of the concerned bank capital. 3. This enhancement of resilience and competitiveness is absolutely necessary in order that national banking is able to face financial sector dynamics. At the level of national dynamic, we are aware that there are still a number of challenges that we must confront together.  First, the structure of national banking needs to be arranged in order to create fairer level of playing field;  Second, bank capitals need to be strengthened in order to be able to operate healthily and efficiently in accordance with the scale and complexity of their business activities;  Third, banks efficiency at present are still relatively low, and therefore needs improvement; and  Fourth, role of banks in intermediation needs to be improved, specifically in the sector of MSME. 4. At the level of regional dynamics, we will encounter integration of ASEAN economic in year 2015 and integration of financial sector in year 2020. In the banking sector, eventually we will encounter Qualified ASEAN Banks (QAB) that have single passport to operate throughout the ASEAN countries. Hence, national banking needs to compete for improving their performances, both from the perspective of financial, capital, risk management and Good Corporate Governance, so as to have high resilience and competitiveness that are capable to become the champion whether at national, regional or global level. 5. To address such various challenges, in the year 2012, Bank Indonesia has issued a series of integrated regulations in order to arrange the structure of Indonesias banking. In addition to PBI Multi-license, PBI Ownership was also issued which aims to restructure the ownership structure of Banks in Indonesia through the application of maximum limit of share ownership. Apart from that, a regulation on Sole Proprietorship in Indonesian Banking was also issued to encourage consolidation of banks business group. Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen Seminar Participants, Challenges in the implementation of regulation on Multi-license 6. As we all know, in the regulation on multi-license, banks are grouped into 4 business activities groups referred to as BUKU-Bank Umum Kegiatan Usaha (Business Activities of Commercial Banks), namely BUKU 1 up to BUKU 4. The higher the core capital of the concerned, the higher the BUKU and the broader the coverage of business activities that can be conducted and the more extensive the office networks that can be opened. 7. Our identification results indicate the presence of several challenges in the implementation of multi-license regulation to arrange bank business activities that we need to face together, among others:  First, banks that have limited core capitals, although have conducted business activities that are more extensive than their BUKU, are required to increase their core capitals in order to be able to run their business activities, or to discontinue the improper business activities. This has impacted particularly on banks in the BUKU 1 or BUKU 2 category with capital requirement of less than Rp1 trillion and between Rp1  Rp5 trillion.  Second, arrangement of business activities coverage is expected to encourage BUKU 1 and BUKU 2 to focus on banks main activities, i.e. collection and distribution of funds through products and activities which are basic in nature. This is the background of restrictions on several business activities of BUKU 1 and BUKU 2 among others, prohibition to make complex derivative transactions and e-banking service that requires investment or high competency of human resources. Meanwhile, BUKU 3 and BUKU 4 categories that conduct a more diverse business activity with higher risk profile or complexity are expected to compete at national level or global, especially in ASEAN countries.  Third, business activities of banks should remain in favor of economic development. Therefore, Bank Indonesia shall determine target of productive credit distribution that should be met by each BUKU. The higher the BUKU, the larger target of productive credit that should be distributed. This target already includes distribution of MSME credits of 20% at a minimum in accordance with the regulation on MSME already issued last year. Pursuant to this regulation, it is expected that intermediation function of Banks can run as it should and the wheel of economy can move rapidly again.  Fourth, arrangement of business activities based on core capital shall impact KCBA (Foreign Bank Branch Office), where the capital core for KCBA is assessed by Capital Equivalence Maintained Asset (CEMA) which must be met in order to be able run business activities conducted at present. CEMA is part of bank business funds that must be pledged in commercial papers in Indonesia that meet certain qualification. Through the fulfillment of CEMA, it is expected that KCBA capital becomes stronger so that it can avoid the negative impact of the crisis abroad or risk exposure from the head office. Ladies and Gentlemen Seminar Participants, Office Network Settings and Access to Finance 8. It cannot be denied that banks constitute of business institutions that in their business activities strive to optimize profits for the interest of the stakeholders especially the shareholders. However, as an intermediation, banking must be further motivated in order to optimally contribute in the economic development, especially in the areas that all this time underserved by banking service. Therefore, mechanism of opening bank office networks must be arranged in such a way to meet the national interest. 9. The arrangement of office networks based on core capital naturally will impact on expansion plan of bank office networks in the years to come, where banks with higher core capital have opportunities to open more extensive office networks, including in opening branches in foreign countries. On the contrary, for banks with lower core capitals will have restrictions in the opening of their office networks. 10. Nevertheless, Bank Indonesia also has a mission to equalize community access to banking services, particularly for areas that have minimum bank office networks. Therefore, Bank Indonesia applies a number of policies in the opening of office networks so that banks can enhance their roles in encouraging economic growth of Indonesia sustainably.  First, Bank Indonesia requires banks in BUKU 3 and BUKU 4 categories to open certain number of offices in the areas with minimum bank office networks (under bank) every time they open office networks in the saturated areas (over bank). Through this obligation, it is expected that access to banking services in the under bank zones can be opened so that in the long run it can promote regional economic growth.  Second, Bank Indonesia shall apply a mechanism of incentive and disincentive for banks that indicate their favor to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSME), through a special treatment (incentive) in opening office networks. Conversely, for banks which MSME credit distributions are still low, they will not get a special treatment in opening office networks. This distribution of MSME credits will be one of Bank Indonesias considerations if allocation of banks core capitals is not sufficient anymore to open office networks.  Third, to encourage efficiency level of banking industry, Bank Indonesia also grants special treatment (incentive) in opening office networks based on supervisory assessment on the achievement of bank efficiency, which among others is reflected through NIM ratio and BOPO (ROA) of banks. Distinguished participants of seminar, closing 11. We are aware that there are still many challenges that must be confronted in order to implement this regulation of multi-license. However, through a good cooperation between banking and Bank Indonesia, we believe that in time eventually we will witness a better Indonesias banking industry, which will be more resilient to crisis, and has a high competitiveness, whether on a national, regional or global scale. 12. This seminar certainly constitutes a good opportunity for all seminar participants to discuss issues around the multi-license regulation. Moreover, as this seminar presents competence speakers in economic and banking sectors, so that I believe the discussions will take place productively. 13. Finally, I would like to congratulate all participants. Hopefully this seminar can improve the understanding on multi-license regulation so that its implementation later on can take place smoothly and the desired objectives to enhance resilience and competitiveness of national banking can be realized. Thank you. Wabillahi taufiq walhidayah, wassalaamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakaatuh. Jakarta, 7 February 2013 Dr. Halim Alamsyah

Title: Keynote Speech by Ronald Waas Deputy Governor of Bank IndonesiainThe2nd Executive Annual Gathering of Indonesia Payment System Association (ASPI), Bali 22 November 2013
text: KEYNOTE SPEECH OF THE DEPUTY GOVERNOR OF BANK INDONESIA IN THE 2ND EXECUTIVE ANNUAL GATHERING OF INDONESIAN PAYMENT SYSTEM ASSOCIATION (ASPI) Bali, 22 November 2013 The Honourable, Board and Members of Indonesian Payment System Association and distinguished guests, Good evening and greetings to all of us, Please allow me to invite all of us to praise God the Almighty for the blessings bestowed upon us so that we have the opportunity to meet in healthy and good condition in Jimbaran, Bali, for the 2nd Executive Annual Gathering of Indonesian Payment System Association (ASPI). I welcome this annual forum, which is the second forum since its establishment in 2010. This forum unquestionably plays a significant role in aligning the direction of payment system development strategy in Indonesia by industries. Approaching the end of 2013, I also wish this meeting serves as the right moment to look back to the journey and development of payment system for the last one year, simultaneously as an event of evaluation, introspection, and learning for all of us. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, Three years since ASPI inauguration is not a short period and we must have done much to improve ASPI as a self-regulatory organization (SRO). However, we also realize that ASPIs role to promote payment system development in Indonesia is not easy and requires many measures, as it is a huge work highly requiring management with our respective functions and authority. In relation thereto, we do hope this forum becomes the right momentum to tie the connection between us, formulate shared perception on reading the economic condition, anticipate challenges ahead, and agree on measures for a much better payment system in Indonesia. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, We feel a wave of uncertainty for the last half decade has been dominating the global economic condition. Such condition creates the so-called New Normal, a period when economic landscape extremely shifts to touch a new, more stable equilibrium. Such drastic change creates a new uncertainty pendulum, so that the new normal phase is finally considered imaginary. A few years ago, the phase is marked with two-speed world recovery, namely economic recovery acceleration divergence between advanced and emerging economies. However, the declining performance of emerging markets with the soft landing of China, and the rising of American and European economy creates three-speed world recovery. Changes in the global economic order affects the movement space and vision of various entities, in global and local financial and non-financial institutions. The Government and Bank Indonesia, as a central bank, closely relate to such changes. Such global economic condition adjustment continuously affects the heartbeat of domestic economy. We feel that 2013 was not an easy year for us. National economy slowed down with lower growth than expected. On the external side, national economic pressure intensified, particularly boosted by a deficit in the Current Transactions. Rupiah exchange rate was significantly adjusted, while inflation surpassed the target of 4.51% due to fuel subsidy reduction and sharp increase in volatile food. Amidst the consistently revolving global economic turbulence, we must be grateful that we survive at a quite high growth level of 5.7%, far above the average growth of peer countries at an estimated level of 3.6%. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, Such challenges must be addressed in line with the approaching commitment to ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) in 2015. AEC is the embodiment of ASEANs communal strategy to become the key player of the global production chain. Deeper integration within ASEAN region will consolidate ASEAN centrality, thereby shifting global economic activity gravity to ASEAN1. On one hand, AEC commitment will open market opportunities with freer flow of goods, services, investment, manpower and capital. However, on the other hand, it also results in stricter competition in the domestic market of each country. With the massive market potential, we observe that the most fundamental substance of AEC commitment is our ability to create competitiveness. Are we capable of using AEC as the key player of global production chain, or do we only become the market target and marginalized? In my opinion, it is at this point our ability to read and anticipate economic movements ahead will be more proven. Survivors are not always the strongest; they are the smartest. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, In relation to payment system growth, we must realize that payment system development potential in Indonesia becomes bigger. There are some factors which I think highly influential to payment system development in Indonesia. First, Indonesia has abundant natural resources and the largest population of 240 million people in South East Asia. IMFs GDP data by purchasing power parity (PPP) also 1 Plummer and Yue (2009) indicates that this year Indonesias GDP has reached USD 1.2 trillion, and it is predicted that Indonesia will overtake some big countries like Australia and Canada. With such a massive economic magnitude, our economic growth rate in the last few years is even far ahead of the average economic growth of peer countries. Second, the profit margin of Indonesias financial industry market structure is quite wide, which is attractive to foreign investors in the world. Goldman Sachs Asset Management, which previously introduced the acronym of BRIC, now introduces a new acronym, i.e. MIST, standing for Mexico, Indonesia, South Korea and Turkey; four country members of G-20 rising as new stars for international investors. Third, middle class society is estimated to grow to 150 million people in 20142, which means more than 50% of Indonesias population is the potential market for payment system. In 2020, the number of Indonesias middle class society is estimated to grow twice from now3. Fourth, the largest portion of our population today is at the age of 0-24 years; therefore, within 20-25 years they will be at their productive age. Such demographic dividend springs more obviously amidst the aging society phase in other countries like Japan and European countries. Expansion of Indonesias middle class society within the next decade will continue and our domestic market will consistently grow. Boom cycle of middle class people will increase purchasing power making consumption trend moves, from products to meet basic needs to products offering convenience and comfort, from durable household furniture to financial services. When we carefully notice this, the middle class people are the biggest users of service sector with cashless shopping characteristics as well as quick, safe, and efficient payment settlement. 2 Nomura, World Bank, CEIC 2012 3 BOG Forecast, March 2013 Such facts must become opportunities and challenges for us to boost payment system growth rate in Indonesia. Bank Indonesia and industries as well as all payment system actors must be committed to realize a safe and efficient payment system. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, Such condition needs a positive response from businesses, associations, the government, and Bank Indonesia as the regulatory body. We need a national strategy supported by all stakeholders. We all need the important role of a secure, efficient, and smooth payment system in the mix of monetary stability policy and financial system stability to support sustainable national economic growth. Coordination and consolidation of policy authority and businesses become more critical since wider business need changes, rapid technology advancement and product innovation, resulting in more complex method and means of payment. In connection therewith, Bank Indonesia as a Payment System Authority is demanded to direct industries to move efficiently; create an enabling climate for payment system and financial transaction settlement; and strengthen customer protection by honouring national interest for payment system providers and customers through provision of a wider and reachable access to the general public. Development of national payment system industry will be made through improvement of payment system architecture including: First, strengthening of domestic industry structure by development of National Payment Gate (GPN). GPN is a must to allow us to play host in our country. It has been a discourse for too long and concrete steps must be taken to realize it. Second, technical standardization and mechanism to increase efficiency. This strategy will be taken to build standardization aspect in national payment system industry. This strategy will realize a safe, smooth system; fair competition will be ensured; and economic rent will be eliminated. In relation to this standardization, I expect that concurrence will be achieved by ASPI, Principal Forum, and Payment System Actors on national standard and the management. ASPI is also expected to prepare a road map and steps approaching 1 January 2016 to become a shared commitment. Bank Indonesia will promote and facilitate to allow implementation of the industrial standardization within the near future as targeted on 1 January 2016 at the latest. We all have started this and it is our obligation to complete it. I realize that something we originally start may have deficiencies, but it is our tasks to cover such deficiencies. Third, expansion of payment service access. This strategy is conducted as an integral part of inclusive financial policy supported by customer education and protection program by using optimum information technology in a more effective manner. Many people still cannot enjoy payment system service and we must be able to answer this challenge by safely and efficiently providing such services to those people. Ladies and gentlemen, Payment system develops rapidly. Various non-cash transactions develop quickly, especially in mobile mode. To realize a holistic efficiency, I am sure the system we build must be able to anticipate and accommodate such development through access expansion for connectivity instruments and infrastructures in digital and physical forms. Payment system instruments must be user-friendly so that people are willing and start to get used to using it. On the other hand, infrastructures must be expanded or added, primarily network operator interconnectivity, thereby people who already have the instruments will be able to use them easily anywhere, anytime. Our perspective on customers must also change. We must be able to adapt to changes and create innovations to win customers hearts. Ten years ago, nobody could predict that 90% of our daily transactions will be electronic; internet banking will give higher revenue than branch offices; social media (facebook, twitter, blog) even becomes the biggest online transaction place in the world. Mobile phones will even replace the role of our physical wallets. Therefore, payment technology utilization will be optimized to serve people in cities and to reach people in remote areas, whose potential development may be accelerated. This development must be implemented through a careful planning to align it to the expected goal by observing all risks. Payment system development may become the main factor to support financial inclusion program at the initial phase of the development. However, inclusion program will be implemented in a selective manner and it has not covered all components, like infrastructure. Payment technology development and remittance are activities to support financial inclusion program. Payment system may also become a very vital means to be able to distribute the work results of our migrant workers for economic activities in Indonesia, primarily in the origins of the workers, through excellent remittance service. For that reason, BI will always strive to expand public access to Payment System service by maintaining public security and convenience in transactions. In the area of remittance, development policy will be made by optimizing the role of existing domestic players, including banks with such ability to provide remittance services. BI realizes that it cannot make the development alone, but it must collaborate with the actors in payment system industry. This development will expand the major stakeholders of BI to include not only banks and non-bank financial institutions, but also actors in telecommunication and information technology industry. We must admit that we are left behind in payment system sector, and we must catch up, particularly in retail payment system, by strengthening regulations, institutions, licensing, and supervision of payment system. Realizing the high public interest in more complex payment transactions, I expect ASPI and BI as the regulatory body will be able to create an enabling climate with the awareness of market actors in the industry on licensing and supervision of payment system. In terms of electronic money, initial steps taken through limited interoperability/ interconnection in banks and between telecommunication providers are the momentum of electronic money growth in Indonesia. In my opinion, electronic money growth can reduce the need for small banknotes, especially coins. It is expected that in the near future, there will be a business model jointly agreed with a clear time target. Once more, technology advancement makes us think that business is not usual, I expect instrument innovation by prioritizing security and efficiency will come into view and at the same time consider the customer protection aspect. Ladies and gentlemen, In cash payment system, BI also faces very heavy challenges, not only in providing cash in good condition, but also in reaching the whole country. We are aware that cash handling cost borne by banks is not cheap. Therefore, cash management starting from distribution to sorting and printing at the central bank incurs high cost and takes much time. Cooperation of all parties in this instance becomes a crucial factor, namely the role of banks as the key player in distributing cash to the general public, regional government, and police helping to secure cash distribution. We must be able to optimize the strength of banks in the form of offices spread throughout Indonesia. BI itself will improve cash distribution pattern, among others by building cash management centres and develop cooperation scheme with many parties. 2014 is an important year in cash management by the Republic of Indonesia in accordance with Law No. 7 of 2011, specifying that on 17 August 2014 Money of the Republic of Indonesia will be issued, which is signed by BI Governor and Finance Minister of the Republic of Indonesia. In addition, Rupiah redenomination is still being prepared while waiting for the right moment in terms of economy, politics, and security. Ladies and gentlemen, At the end of my speech this morning, I would like to remind all of us to move forward in a strategic manner and together become the best in the region. We must be able to become a market sharper, instead of a market follower, especially in Asian market. Second, on the growth rate of non-cash transactions, I expect the value will increase twice of GDP in 2014. To achieve this, it is a fundamental prerequisite to change public paradigm to use non-cash for it is more efficient, quicker, and safer. It is our responsibility to educate the general public to increase transactions by using non-cash means of payment. Finally, I would like to extend my appreciation of the hard work for organizing this gathering, which is expected to produce fresh ideas as a concrete breakthrough in creating a better national payment system. Small minds discuss people, average minds discuss events, great minds discuss ideas4. 4 Eleanor Roosevelt I am also looking forward to the presentation of ASPI homework, especially on NSICCS, so that we can realize a safe and efficient payment system with the implemented global challenges-global solutions. The future of Indonesia depends on us all. Thank you. Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia Ronald Waas

Title: Conference Series on Managing Inflation: Railway-Based Food Logistics System (Keynote Speech by Ronald Waas Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia) Bandung, 26 March 2014
text: KEYNOTE SPEECH OF THE DEPUTY GOVERNOR OF BANK INDONESIA Conference Series on Managing Inflation: Railway-Based Food Logistics System Bandung, 26 March 2014 The Honourable, - Vice Governor of West Java, - Heads of Universities, - Representatives of the relevant Ministries (Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs, Transportation Ministry, Agriculture Ministry, and Trade Ministry), - Resource Persons, The Distinguished, - Heads of Representative Offices of Bank Indonesia, - Representatives of Regional Inflation Control Teams in Java, - Businesses and Associations, - Ladies and Gentlemen, Good morning and greetings to all of us, 1. Let us praise God the Almighty for the blessings bestowed upon us so that we have the opportunity to gather today in a healthy and favourable condition to attend the Conference Series on Managing Inflation: Railway-Based Food Logistics System in the Bank Indonesia Representative Office of Region VI (West Java and Banten). 2. I welcome and appreciate the Regional Inflation Control Team of West Java Province, Padjadjaran University, and Bank Indonesia Representative Office of Region VI for initiating this event. 3. This national conference is the appropriate forum to exchange thoughts and level perception among policy makers, academicians, and businesses. I expect todays discussion will produce solutions and set comprehensive and synergic action plans to address problems we face, primarily pertaining to inflation control from food aspect. 4. Todays discussion will become sharper and more complete because the Vice Governor of West Java is present among us as well as various parties and resource persons representing the government, Bank Indonesia, academicians, practitioners, businesses, associations, mass media, and Regional Inflation Control Team in Java. Your attendance confirms that food logistics in inflation control efforts suit our concern. 5. We experience a strong uncertainty in the global economy within the last half decade. The drastic change of global economic structure continuously creates a new uncertainty pendulum. Global economic growth slowdown, including in China, results in decreasing export demand and commodity prices. The Feds Quantitative Easing policy also causes high uncertainty affecting fluctuation of rupiah exchange rate. 6. 2013 was not an easy year for us. National economy slowed down with lower growth than expected. On the external side, national economic pressure intensified, particularly boosted by a deficit in the Current Transactions. Rupiah exchange rate was significantly adjusted, while inflation surpassed the target of 4.51% due to fuel subsidy reduction and sharp increase in volatile food. 7. Amidst the consistently revolving global economic turbulence, we must be grateful that we survive at a quite high growth level of 5.7%, far above the average growth of peer countries at an estimated level of 3.6%. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, 8. The diverse challenges must be observed in line with the approaching commitment to the 2015 ASEAN Economic Community (AEC). On one hand, AEC commitment will open market opportunities with freer flow of goods, services, investment, manpower, and capital. However, on the other hand, it also brings the consequence of stronger competition in the domestic market of respective countries. 9. I am confident that the most fundamental substance of AEC commitment is our ability to create competitiveness and become the key player of global production chain, instead of becoming the market target and marginalized. In my opinion, it is at this point our ability to read and anticipate economic movements ahead will be more proven. Survivors are not always the strongest; they are the smartest. 10. In response to the challenges, Bank Indonesia focuses on inflation expectation control policy to return inflation to its normal pattern and to achieve inflation target in 2014, i.e. 4.51%. 11. We also put priority on economic stability and growth quality for more stable and balanced economy. Economy in 2014 is projected to grow within the range of 5.5-5.9%. Bank Indonesia also consistently cooperates with the government to return macro stability and strengthen financial stability. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, 12. As we all understand, our domestic inflation is very susceptible to shocks, primarily from the supply side, and administered prices. 13. We witness inflation in 2013 recorded another double digits, far above its normal pattern of 6-7%, especially due to food price fluctuation. Such food price fluctuation results from: (1) Lacking supply of some horticultural commodities due to weather anomaly and limited domestic production; (2) Obstacles in implementation of horticulture and beef import administration policy; (3) Oligopolistic market structure and unclear price information; and (4) High distribution cost due to insufficient infrastructure. 14. I am very pleased to know that our conference today precisely leads us to address some major issues mentioned above and find solutions to reduce the food price fluctuation. Distribution strengthening by railway is one of the favourable breakthroughs and worth support from all parties. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, 15. Food is often strongly related to the aspects of price, availability, and affordability. Food price fluctuation is frequently affected by domestic structural issues, such as limited food production availability, long chain of logistics and supply, high transportation cost, land function change, and inefficient infrastructure. 16. Based on its contribution to GDP, performance of national agricultural sector tends to decrease from 13.2% in 2010 to 12.3% in 2013. Such decrease is in line with the increasing national food import. Meanwhile, on inflation side, food contributes more than 50% to CPI inflation today. Food inflation pressure in 2013 is recorded 9.7%, higher than non-food inflation of 7.1%. 17. We cannot deny that food management is a huge work for us. Global Food Security Index (GFSI) in 2013 released by Economic Intelligent Unit shows that Indonesias food security index ranks 66th out of 107 countries. Moreover, in ASEAN region, national food security ranks sixth, behind Thailand, Vietnam, and Philippines. 18. Such weak national food security is also reflected from Indonesias inflation rate which is higher than other ASEAN countries, such as Malaysia, Philippines, and Thailand. National Logistics System still ranks sixth in ASEAN region. 19. This inadequate logistics system results in high logistics cost. Based on the data from the Transportation Ministry, logistics cost in Indonesia is still high, reaching 24% of the goods price. The figure is much higher than that of other countries like Malaysia with only 15%. Furthermore, AGRILocics of Agriculture Socioeconomic Department of Padjadjaran University calculates that food logistics cost in Indonesia reaches 55%. 20. It is related to the dominant use of road transportation in Indonesias logistics system. Around 80% of transportation movement in Java Island is dominated by road transportation. This condition highly affects inflation control efforts owing to high dependency on only road transportation. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, 21. From such condition, I think a comprehensive and collaborative policy among all parties is not enough to solve problems pertaining to food security. Breakthroughs are needed to accelerate food self-sufficiency structure and foundation, primarily related to food logistics system. 22. Breakthroughs are also needed to balance transportation load. One of the breakthroughs is optimizing use of railway to transport agricultural products. Train is an efficient and relatively cheap transportation mode compared to other modes. With the present infrastructure spread through stations in major cities and agricultural producers in Java Island, use of railway for food logistics must be optimized. In addition to promoting more smooth food distribution, transportation cost in a certain volume will also decrease. 23. However, we must realize that food logistics system implementation by railway still faces many obstacles, such as unfulfilled scale of economy of farmers products against the number and volume of cars per trip, guaranteed cargo from train departure until its arrival, and warehouse logistics system in production centres and sale centres, which are far located and inaccessible directly from the station. 24. Therefore, use of goods train should be adjusted to supply chain management for food products. Establishment or empowerment of Farmer Group Association (Gapoktan) and Breeder Group Association (Gapoknak) and establishment of hub warehouse can support to fulfil scale of economy of transportation volume of agricultural and farming products. This warehouse may also be combined with Warehouse Receipt system which may simultaneously be used for farmer financing. Going forward, this synergy is also expected to be able to boost increase in post-harvest technology, including packing and warehouse with cold storage system. 25. Trade cooperation between regions can also be optimized through cooperation of Regional Inflation Control Team (TPID), particularly areas with railways, such as Surabaya, Semarang, Yogyakarta, Cirebon, Bandung, Karawang, Bekasi, Banten, Jakarta, etc. This is in line with one of the recommendations of National Working Team of TPID 2013 to intensify trade cooperation between regions. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished guests, 26. Observing the importance of the problems mentioned above, I am confident that we share the same opinion that we need to strengthen infrastructure development, which supports railway-based food supply chain system as the implementation of national logistics system. This is done not only in the context of inflation control and food security but also in an effort to increase national competitiveness through national food logistics system. 27. Through this conference, I expect we manage to produce an action plan of a practicable multi-year railway-based food logistics system. I also hope that a close collaboration between policy makers, academicians, and businesses in realizing this action plan ahead may be consistently improved to find solutions to fundamental issues faced by this nation. 28. We conclude our speech as an introduction to the discussion in the Conference Series on Managing Inflation: Railway-Based Food Logistics System. May you have a fruitful discussion. Thank you. Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia Ronald Waas

Title: Bank Indonesias Policy on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement:PublicLecturebyHendar, Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia, Kediri, March 27, 2015
text: POINTERS OF PUBLIC LECTURE MATERIAL Bank Indonesias Policy on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement Dr Hendar Deputy Governor of Bank Indonesia Bismillaahirrohmaanirrohiim Assalaamualaikum warahmatullaahi wabarakaatuh Good morning and may God bless us all 1. To start todays public lecture, let us praise God the Almighty for the blessings bestowed upon us so that todays public lecture on central banks may run well. 2. My presentation in todays public lecture is divided into 3 (three) major parts. First, I will briefly explain the main tasks and functions of Bank Indonesia as a central bank. Second, I will discuss financial inclusion in an in-depth manner. After this lecture, I expect you to understand what financial inclusion is, why it is important in terms of monetary policies and poverty alleviation, and how it is practiced in various countries. In the third part, I will explain the strategies and policies of Bank Indonesia to encourage the adoption of financial inclusion. In this lecture, I will emphasize such adoption primarily through NonCash National Movement. Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished students, The Position and Main Tasks and Functions of Bank Indonesia (slide 4) 3. In the first part, I will start by explaining the position as well as main tasks and functions of Bank Indonesia. The position of Bank 1 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement Indonesia as a central bank independent of performing its tasks and authority has started upon enforcement of Law No. 23/1999 on Bank Indonesia on 17 May 1999 as amended by Law No. 6/2009. Bank Indonesia has full autonomy to formulate and perform its tasks and authority. 4. External parties are not allowed to interfere in the performance of Bank Indonesias tasks, and Bank Indonesia is obliged to refuse or overlook interventions in any forms from any parties. In its capacity as a central bank, Bank Indonesia has the sole objective to achieve and maintain the stability of rupiah. Rupiah stability has two aspects, namely stability against goods and services, and stability against other currencies. The first aspect is reflected on inflation rate, while the second is reflected on rupiah exchange rate against other currencies. The formulation of this sole objective aims to explicate targets to be achieved by Bank Indonesia as well as the limits of its responsibilities. 5. To achieve such objective, Bank Indonesia is supported by three pillars as its three tasks, namely monetary stability, financial system stability, and payment system stability. The three tasks must be integrated to achieve the objective and maintain rupiah stability in an effective and efficient manner. 6. In monetary stability pillar, Bank Indonesia has a duty to maintain monetary stability, among others through the instrument of interest rate in an open market operation. Bank Indonesia is demanded to be able to establish appropriate and balanced monetary policies. The reason is disrupted monetary stability directly affects various economic aspects. A monetary policy on applying a too stringent interest rate will tend to stop economic activities. And the other way around. Therefore, to establish monetary stability, Bank Indonesia has adopted a policy called inflation targeting framework. 2 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement 7. The enforcement of the Law on Financial Services Authority (OJK) in 2011 has opened a new chapter in the history of Bank Indonesia. Regulatory and supervisory tasks on banks previously performed by Bank Indonesia have been transferred to OJK since 31 December 2013. However, through its authority, Bank Indonesia still contributes to maintain the stability of Indonesias financial system, primarily from macroprudential aspect. In this pillar, Bank Indonesia carries out surveillance of various indicators considered as threats to financial stability. Through macroprudential monitoring, Bank Indonesia may monitor financial sector vulnerability and detect potential shock affecting financial system stability. Bank Indonesia can develop macroprudential instruments and indicators to detect such financial sector vulnerability. Results of such research and monitoring will then serve as a recommendation for Bank Indonesia in applying macroprudential policies and for the relevant authorities in taking appropriate measures to curb financial sector disruptions. One of the policies of Bank Indonesia in this pillar is the Loan To Value policy for vehicle and house ownership, which is effective in curbing an increase in property price as well as vehicle credit extension risks. 8. In the payment system stability pillar, Bank Indonesia has the authority to control and maintain smooth payment system. If failure to settle occurs to one of the participants in the payment system, severe potential risks may arise and disrupt smooth payment system. Such failure may result in contagious risks leading to systemic disruption. Bank Indonesia develops a mechanism and arrangement to reduce heightened risks in the payment system. Financial Inclusion-Why is it important? 3 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished students, 9. The second part of this public lecture will explain what and how financial inclusion is. Financial inclusion has become a trending topic in the financial world, both conventional and sharia, national and international. Global financial crisis in 2008 reminds us of the essence of financial sector in the economy. Does financial sector actually play an important role in supporting the economy for all people? Or, is it only meeting the demand to make increasingly higher profit, which puts the original objective away? 10. In this part, we will discuss why financial inclusion is important and therefore needs particular attention. In slide 6, we find that financial services in Indonesia still lag behind, especially outside Java Island. Based on the ratio of the number of ATMs per 100 thousand adults and the number of bank offices per 100 thousand adults, there is a wide gap between Java and other islands. For example, in Jakarta, there are 71 ATMs and 213 bank offices per 100 thousand people. Meanwhile, there are only 17 ATMs and 27 bank offices in Central Kalimantan. In the Eastern Part of Indonesia, the number is smaller; for example, East Nusa Tenggara only has 15 ATMs and 16 bank offices. 11. Moving on to the next slide, we also find that financial exclusion in Indonesia is still high. The World Banks data in the 2011 Global Financial Inclusion Index defines that only 20% adults in Indonesia have accounts in formal financial institutions. Compared to our closest neighbors, like the Philippines with 26.5%, we also lag behind them. Not to mention India (35.2%) and China (63.8%). Meanwhile, India and China have more population than Indonesia. 12. The World Banks indicator at household level also describes the same. The survey says that 68% households have savings and only 48% have savings with formal financial institutions. From the 4 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement borrowers side, 60% households may make borrowings. One serious concern is only 17% financing comes from banks, while 36% comes from non-formal financial institutions. 13. The survey result is in line with bank credit indicators. Low MSME credit access is reflected on low MSME credit segment, which is less than 20%. Through more in-depth observation, credit segment for micro sector turns out to be lower, less than 19%. On the other hand, the interest rate of MSME credit is considered high, above 15%. The fact is more than 90% businesses in Indonesia are MSMEs. It then creates more constraints for MSMEs to obtain financial supports. 14. In slide 8, we see that limited financial access also correlates to the increasing gap level. High economic growth (as indicated by increasing GDP/capita) should be followed by gini ratio decrease. However, the fact is reversed, where the correlation of gini ratio and GDP/capita is parallel. This is confirmed by the decreasing number of low income people against GDP growth, where such number has been decreasing since 2009 amidst more steady economic growth above 6%. If we compare financial sector access of Indonesia to various countries as seen in the table below, it is indicated that limited financial access cannot transmit economic growth to unbanked people, which further prevents poverty alleviation. 15. In the next slide, it may be seen that Indonesia still falls in the category of countries with high cash transactions (cash-based economy). Based on the chart, Indonesia sits in the lower group with Nigeria in terms of non-cash transactions. From the financial inclusion perspective, cash transactions make economic actors unable to have any incentive to enter the financial sector. This is also supported by consumptive behavior and limited income for savings. Consequently, economic actors have never been recorded as the customers of financial 5 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement institutions. Meanwhile, financial record is one of the important prerequisites for credit extension, which may boost economic activities. Why is unbanked people level high? 16. Then, why is unbanked people level in Indonesia still high? The World Banks survey catches 2 sides of demand and supply. On the supply side, there are several factors inhibiting services to the community, such as costly branch establishment, complex establishment process, high degree of formality, banks perception of unprofitable grassroots customers, and unsupportive IT such as limited and inefficient communication network. Those factors result in banks decisions to prefer to enter mature areas, such as Java Island and big cities outside Java. 17. Meanwhile, on the demand side, there are some inhibiting factors: insufficient money for savings, expensive fees, far distance from houses to bank offices, lack of understanding on saving money with banks, no documents as required like resident's identity cards, distrust in banking system, or religious reasons. International Trend towards Financial Inclusion Ladies and gentlemen, and distinguished students, 18. Seeing that financial access in Indonesia still lags behind other countries as previously explained, we note that Indonesia is not the only country with such concern. Developed and developing countries also pay particular attention to increase their financial inclusion. 19. In slide 14, we can see various financial inclusion policies in various countries. In England, banks provide credit, financial advice, and nofrills accounts, which are savings accounts without any administrative fees. In the United States, through Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), prohibition of discrimination against small account holders (with 6 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement minimum balance of 0.10) applies. In India, bank network expansion efforts are made through the use of business correspondents (agents). 20. Based on best practices in financial access expansion, there are 2 big models, namely telco-based and bank-based. By telcobased practice, telco companies become the leader in providing the most fundamental bank services. In this model, telco companies issue electronic money and save assets in an equal value thereto in combined accounts with the bank. 21. Meanwhile, by bank-based model, banks serve financial services needed by the community. In this model, there are 3 schemes. First, banks provide individual accounts which can be used through branchless channels they manage, such as CAIXA in Brazil, bKash in Bangladesh, and Telenor in Pakistan. Second, banks provide individual accounts accessible by agents and managed by non-banks and/or through the technology, like SMART (21 banks in the Philippines). Third, banks issue electronic money for direct sale and distribution by non-banks to customers. 22. Each of the approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. Telcobased model will be preferable if speed, wide coverage, mass market grasp, and many agents are the priority. However, this model has some weaknesses due to the absence of deposit insurance by LPS, no interest for the e-money, and low credit extension potential. 23. If convenience becomes the priority (existence of consumer protection, regulation by the authority, deposit insurance by LPS, and interest), bank-based model is the option. However, this model also has some weaknesses in terms of speed, limited access, and high cost. 24. In the next slide, we can see that Mobile Money or Electronic Money has quite expansive development in the international world. The rapid 7 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement growth of telecommunication sector is considered to support electronic money development. In the implementation of this model, focus on unbanked people is given to almost all developing and poor countries. Until 2013, there are 219 implementations of mobile money in 84 countries. Why does BI have to be present in promoting financial inclusion? 25. In the third part of my presentation, financial inclusion is found to be highly relevant to support effective functions and tasks of Bank Indonesia in terms of monetary aspect, payment system, and macroprudence. In terms of financial system stability, financial inclusion helps reduce pressures from liquidity risk and credit risk in banking sector. From liquidity aspect, banks gain relatively stable retail fund sources even in shocks. From credit aspect, new retail markets open, primarily micro and small credits, endorsing diversification of portfolios and credit risks. Financial inclusion programs further help increase communitys capability with the resulting financial responsibilities after implementation of financial education and consumer protection programs. 26. From monetary policy aspect, with financial inclusion, policy rate can touch the community at all levels in any places because policy rate is transmitted through banks, thereby supporting to realize effective monetary policies and the community will not be affected by the second round effect of the policies. 27. Meanwhile, from payment system aspect, smoother payment system to the whole areas leads to the common use by wider community wherever they are. In addition, less cash society program may be implemented with added value for the community and economy. What are the strategies of Bank Indonesia? 8 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement 28. In encouraging financial inclusion, Bank Indonesia adopts strategies by emphasizing implementation through payment system aspect, by educating people at the bottom of the pyramid to learn to keep their money from cash-based in the house to account-based in electronic money accounts. It may help reduce consumptive tendency and serve as the initial point of financial diary, managing simple finance supported by financial education programs. Through BI roles in financial inclusion, it is expected that the capability and life quality of people at the bottom of the pyramid will improve. It may also support to alleviate poverty and gain demographic dividend because of the high productive age in Indonesia now and in the future. 29. The financial inclusion program of Bank Indonesia closely relates to Bank Indonesias efforts to realize transformation from inefficient cash society, marked by high printing cost of approximately Rp 3 trillion/year, small money in hand, much time to count the change, and difficulty in keeping much cash, to less cash society identical to the use of safe and efficient electronic money, credit cards, and debit cards with a wider access. 30. Bank Indonesia and the relevant institutions (the Coordinating Ministry of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance, DKI Jakarta Province Government, and the Association of Indonesian Province Governments) as well as industry actors in payment system under the Association of Payment System in Indonesia (ASPI) have launched Non-Cash National Movement (GNNT) on 14 August 2014. 31. The GNNT initiative aims to encourage and expand the use of noncash transactions to increase economic efficiency, security, and convenience in transactions, strengthen transparency and accountability, and support efforts to prevent corruption, money laundering, and terrorism funding. Efforts to realize expanded use of 9 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement non-cash transactions are made not only for retail transactions, but also for high value transactions to facilitate financial revenue and expense transactions of corporations and the government. 32. Six priority programs in GNNT initiative closely relate to financial inclusion, namely service expansion through telco network, synergy of banks and non-banks, e-commerce services, public and government services in 34 ministries, regional government services, and the services of state owned enterprises (SOE) and regional owned enterprises (ROE). 33. GNNT aims to increase public awareness of the use of non-cash instruments to gradually establish less cash society (LCS), particularly in making transactions in their economic activities. As a form of our commitment to the expanded use of non-cash instruments, we will make GNNT as an annual movement with various activities to increase public understanding on the use of non-cash instruments in making payment transactions. 34. E-payment has a relatively huge potential for further development. As presented in slide 24, we see as an example the huge potential of transportation sector in Jakarta of 23.4 trillion/year. TransJakarta buses carry 320 thousand passengers every day with an annual turnover of Rp 680 billion. Electric trains as the veins of transportation in Jakarta can carry 400 thousand passengers per day with an annual turnover of Rp 1.4 trillion. The biggest potential is fuel expense in gas stations, which, with an assumed consumption of 1-4 liter per vehicle per day, will reach Rp 14.6 trillion per year. 35. In the next slide, some GNNT programs conducted by various institutions are presented. E-ticketing of Jakarta commuter trains has been interconnected to 4 electronic money of 4 banks. The social aid 10 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement for Family Hope Program has been distributed by electronic money and also through DFS agents. Healthy Indonesia Cards and Smart Indonesia Cards have also been distributed by using electronic money. To increase the local revenue of Jakarta, e-payment has been implemented for retribution of street vendors and e-parking. If you wish to ride on TransJakarta buses, you must also use electronic money. GNNT is also a part of services program for Indonesian migrant workers by the Ministry of Manpower and BNP2TKI through payment of placement and protection services for Indonesian migrant workers and financial education program for Indonesian migrant workers and their families. Going forward, it is also encouraged that remittance in relation to Indonesian migrant workers is made through electronic money. It aims to help reduce the relatively high remittance cost borne by Indonesian migrant workers. 36. Various cooperation and facilitation by Bank Indonesia have been consistently made to encourage cash services. In the following year, we have recorded synergy with 11 Ministries and 34 province governments. We record 5 forms of BI facilities related to non-cash services, namely: mapping of available non-cash services forms, preparation of business model and business process, facilitation of non-cash services availability with industries, and implementation of non-cash services and education. 37. To provide some description of types of non-cash means of payment, slide 26 presents some of the examples. Overall, there are 2 big groups: paper-based and card-based. Paper-based includes checks, giro biljet, and debit notes. Meanwhile, electronic-based among others includes ATM/debit cards, electronic money, credit cards, and mobile money. 11 Public Lecture on the Central Bank - Bank Indonesias Policies on Financial Inclusion through Non-Cash National Movement 38.
